text: Morning email to all staff: “As of Monday, there is no office. We are now fully remote.” Below is a link to a survey: “How do you feel about this?” What do you tick?
Facilities says the office is closing and everyone can take one thing home. Left: a very expensive office chair and the giant ficus everyone watered on a rota. Your pick?
First remote Monday. The alarm goes off at 7:00 like always, even though there’s nowhere to commute to. The first call is two hours away. How do you spend them?
right: Go for a run and eat breakfast

text: The team lead launches a “morning check-in”: at 9:00 everyone posts three words about their mood. So far you’ve woken up enough for two words: “still” and “asleep.” What do you post?
You sit down to work, but the cat has already claimed your chair and is looking at you like this is his office now. Call starts in five minutes. Who gives way?
The company has sent a “remote starter kit”: webcam, headset and a branded hoodie. The courier needs a signature, and you’re wearing duck-print pyjama bottoms. Open the door?
Today’s calendar has seven back-to-back calls with no gaps. The first one is “How not to burn out while remote,” 90 minutes long. What do you do?
8:45. Your upstairs neighbour starts renovating: hammer drill, pause, hammer drill. At 9:00 you have a call with a new client. Your plan?
right: Take the call in the car outside

text: New rule: your chat status must be green from 9 to 6. Five minutes without moving the mouse and it turns yellow, and your manager gets notified. How do you cope?
Mom has learned you work from home now and calls at 9:15: “You’re at home anyway, just pop to the post office for my parcel.” Your stand-up is in ten minutes.
right: Explain that home is work now

text: The new camera switches on in astonishing detail. It shows every pore, every speck of dust on the monitor and a tower of unwashed mugs behind you. Morning planning starts in a minute.
right: Lean in so my face covers it all

text: A colleague in a time zone seven hours ahead messages you at 7:10 your time: “Need an answer urgently, half my day is gone and I’m still waiting.” Your eyes aren’t fully open yet.
The router is blinking red this morning. Rebooting doesn’t help. The provider promises a technician “sometime between 9 and 6.” At 10:00 you’re presenting to the board.
right: Ask to borrow the neighbour’s Wi-Fi

text: The company launched a “commute” app: 15 minutes of recorded metro noise each morning “to help your brain switch over.” The manager asks who has “arrived.”
Your daughter asks for a lift to school since you’re “not at work anymore anyway.” At 9:00 there’s a mandatory all-hands with leadership. School is twenty minutes away.
left: Join the call from the car
right: Ask someone else to drive her

text: Accounting announces an internet allowance: 500 roubles a month, but you need a scan of your provider contract and six months of receipts. The contract is in a box somewhere from the last move.
At the coworking space, the person settling in at the next desk has a rival company’s logo on his mug. Your strategy call starts in 10 minutes.
A new hire started remotely on day one. He messages you: “Sorry, who’s who here? Everyone in chat has a cat as their avatar.” The team lead is busy.
right: Send him the org chart link

text: The company has installed a tracker that screenshots your screen every ten minutes. A pancake recipe from last night is still open. The next screenshot is due any second.
Your partner also works from home, and you both have calls at 9:00. There’s one room with a door, and the kitchen with a humming fridge. Who goes where?
The kettle starts whistling the moment you unmute at stand-up. The whole team hears the shriek. The host goes silent.
The boss on a call: “Go on, share your screen.” Among your tabs: flats in another city, job listings and a chat with a former colleague. You have to share right now.
The designer posts a mockup in chat: “Well?” You react with a 👍. A minute later: “Got it. I’ll redo it.” Apparently your thumbs-up read as passive aggression.
left: Write a long gush of praise

text: A call with the project manager. You spend forty seconds passionately explaining your fix, then notice the banner: “Your microphone is muted.” Everyone waits politely.
On the shared online board with the annual plan, someone has drawn a moustache and hat on the CEO’s photo. The board goes up on a big call in 10 minutes.
The doorbell rings during a client call. It’s your lunch delivery. The dog starts barking his head off, and the client asks: “Everything OK over there?” What do you do?
right: Apologise and step out a minute

text: Gena is always off camera and answers with a couple of minutes’ lag. People whisper in DMs that he has a second job. He asks you to cover for him on a call.
1:00 pm. Remote life has no canteen, and the fridge holds only mustard and half a lemon. The next call starts in 30 minutes. How do you eat?
Grandma is visiting and figures that since you’re home, you can chat. She sits right beside you during a meeting and waves at your colleagues on camera.
right: Gently send her to the kitchen

text: Your “cosy library” virtual background is glitching: every time you move, half your head vanishes. Colleagues have started taking screenshots.
left: Turn it off and show the mess
right: Sit perfectly still till the end

text: The analyst DMs “Got a minute?” and then vanishes for forty minutes. You spend all forty wondering whether you’re being fired or just asked for a spreadsheet password.
You go to a coworking space to work. Every window seat is taken; the only free desk is next to the coffee machine, which grinds beans like a cement mixer every three minutes.
Your manager asks you to record every call “just in case” and upload it to a shared folder. You realise your remark “this project is a swamp” would end up there too.
Your son wanders over during a call and asks loudly: “Is that the lady you said was a pain?” The mic, alas, is on.
A colleague set a new virtual background and asks the chat to rate it out of ten. It’s a photo of himself in front of himself.
Your laptop has overheated from three calls in a row and roars like a jet taking off. Colleagues ask if you’re at the airport. Two more calls to go.
left: Prop it on a cold baking tray

text: Olga from marketing suggests a call “for five minutes, just to discuss.” You know Olga’s five minutes is a standard hour. The question could be answered in one line of chat.
left: Answer in one line of chat

text: A client sent you a gift hamper at the old office address. The new tenants — a bakery — ate it and sent you a grateful photo.
The team lead decides chat feels “too dry” and asks everyone to end every message with an emoji. You’re writing an incident report about a server outage.
On the online brainstorming board, twelve people are dragging sticky notes at once. Someone has shoved your best idea into a corner and covered it with a cat picture.
Power is cut in your building for two hours while they replace the fuse board. Laptop at 34%, phone at 12%. Work and calls carry on.
Marat is arguing with you in the team chat about whether the report title needs a full stop or a comma. The thread is at 63 messages and the lawyer has joined in.
On the all-hands, all forty people have cameras off. The host asks: “Are you there? Type a plus.” Exactly three pluses appear. Are you one of them?
Mid-presentation, your video freezes on a frame of you mouth open, eyes rolled back. The audio continues, the picture doesn’t. Thirty people are looking at this.
left: Carry on as if nothing happened

text: 7:40 pm. You realise you haven’t left your desk since noon. The workday never seems to end when home and office are the same room. How do you call it a day?
left: Throw a towel over the laptop

text: Sveta messages at 9 pm: “Not urgent, just so I don’t forget.” It’s her fourth “not urgent” of the evening. Replying means working; not replying feels awkward.
Friday evening online team building: a team quiz at 7 pm. Your team of five has two people with no sound and one with no internet. You’re captain by default.
While you finish your evening report, the cat brings a sock and drops it on the keyboard. It’s his daily “time to stop” ritual. He’s insistent.
right: Finish with the cat in my arms

text: Your partner says: “We spent the whole day in the same flat and I never saw you.” You were in the next room on calls all day. The report still needs checking tonight.
The neighbours invite you to a barbecue in the courtyard. You promised a colleague in another time zone you’d be reachable till 10 pm “just in case.” Phone in pocket.
The company adopted a “right to disconnect”: no messages to colleagues after 7 pm. At 7:15 on the very first evening, a message arrives — from the policy’s author.
Someone posts a meme about the department head in the evening chat. A minute later, the department head gets added to the chat. The meme is still sitting right above.
You signed up for the gym just to get out of the house sometimes. Training is at 7:30 pm, but at 7:10 the team lead books a call “literally ten minutes.”
You realise you haven’t taken off your pyjamas in three days. They’re great for work, but tonight you’re invited out. Suddenly all your jeans feel tight and hostile.
Your child wants help with maths homework, but at 8 pm you have a call with a team on the other side of the country. It’s the one about two trains heading toward each other.
At 10:30 pm the company bot pings: “Don’t forget to log today’s hours!” You’re already in bed. Skip it and the bot tells your manager.
At 11 pm your time a colleague nine hours ahead writes “good morning!” — his day has just begun. Below it: a request for a report by 8 am your time.
Your workspace is an ironing board in the bedroom. In the evening it’s supposed to turn back into an ironing board, and the bedroom into a bedroom. You’re out of energy to keep shuffling.
A friend invites you to a café: “You’ve been stuck inside all day, come see some humans.” It’s true, the only thing you’ve talked to all day is a monitor. But tomorrow is a deadline.
Text from the provider: “Scheduled maintenance 9 am to 1 pm.” Your quarterly budget defence call is at 10:30. You have two gigabytes of mobile data left.
At the coworking space, the guy at the next desk hosts a loud morning call about “personal productivity.” Today he’s said “step out of your comfort zone” five times already.
left: Ask him to keep it down

text: The team lead, four hours ahead, has set stand-up for 8 am your time: “It’s midday for me, works for everyone.” It doesn’t work for everyone. Do you object?
Before a morning call you catch the mirror: your hair is sticking up like a cartoon scientist. Two minutes to join, no hat in reach.
left: Slick it with water and go

text: The manager decided to hold morning planning in virtual reality and mailed everyone headsets. Five minutes in, you walk into a wardrobe and your avatar drifts through a wall.
Morning in the department chat: “guys, does anyone have access to the finance folder? URGENT!!!” Only you and the chief accountant have access, and she’s on holiday.
Your partner switches on the vacuum at 8:58, “while you’re not on a call.” Your call started at 8:55; you were just listening quietly. Now everyone is listening to the vacuum.
Vlada asks the whole team to switch calendars to her time zone “for simplicity.” Now your stand-up shows as 6:00 and lunch as 17:00.
Anya, in another time zone, asks you to review mockups before her lunch. Her lunch is your 6:30 am. She adds: “Later is fine too, but then I lose a day.”
HR handed out “smart mugs” that count coffee and feed a “wellbeing dashboard.” Yours reports you’ve had 11 cups.
Your camera switches itself on when you start the laptop. You notice when you see your yawning face in the preview of a chat with half the department in it.
Every morning Vika posts a photo of her breakfast in the team chat: “Good morning, team!” Today she tags you directly: “Where’s your breakfast?”
left: Snap a photo of my sandwich

text: Your kitchen chair has been your office chair for two months. In the mornings your back wakes up before the alarm. There’s an office chair on sale, but money’s tight.
A client on the other side of the world writes at 6 am: “A call at 6:30 works for you, right?” He doesn’t seem to realise it’s still night for you. The contract is big.
left: Get up and take the call

text: The coworking manager announces: “Meeting rooms are bookable only!” You booked one for 2 pm, but students are in there pitching a sock-delivery startup.
right: Take the call in the corridor

text: You replied “ok.” with a full stop. Your colleague asks: “Are you upset with me?” You’re not; you just end sentences with full stops.
The account manager has booked a “quick sync” at 1 pm. It’s your only lunch break, and the flat has smelled of meatballs for half an hour.
Your manager says he wants “results, not hours.” A week later he asks why you were offline from 2 to 4 on Tuesday. You were at the dentist.
Your sister came over to “sit quietly while you work” and has spent an hour telling you about her holiday. At 3 pm you need to focus on a report.
You’ve been invited to speak at an online conference. The organiser asks for “studio lighting.” All you’ve got is a desk lamp and your phone’s torch.
While sharing his screen, Petya accidentally shows his chat with you, in which you complained about your manager an hour ago. It’s visible for three seconds, and the manager is on the call.
The courier buzzes mid-call: “It’s heavy, come down yourself.” It’s the new monitor you’ve waited a month for.
right: Ask him to leave it with the concierge

text: A shared online spreadsheet: you spent two hours entering figures while someone else sorted it alphabetically. Your data is now mixed up with everyone else’s.
Your kid comes home from school bursting to tell you about a top mark. You’re on a call. He’s standing there with his school diary, beaming. The client call has been going for an hour.
The accountant sends a spreadsheet: “take a look 🙂.” For the first time you’re unsure: is that a polite smile or “look what you’ve done”?
The company has paid for your online course “Effective Remote Work.” It’s 40 hours, during work time. Nobody moved the project deadline.
Your neighbour knocks: his internet is down and he wants your Wi-Fi password “literally for an hour.” Your bandwidth already struggles with calls.
The team lead proposes a “virtual office”: an app where everyone sits at desks as avatars and can walk up to each other. Within an hour your avatar is stuck in the lift.
right: Park my avatar in a corner

text: Mid-discussion your voice suddenly turns robotic, like an old alien movie. Colleagues ask you to “say it again, but as a human.”
For a week Timur has replied to everything with voice notes. Even a yes-or-no question gets a minute-long recording with metro noise in the background.
The client asks to talk “right now, no cameras, just voice.” A minute in, it turns out nine more people from his side are on the call, all with cameras on.
HR is throwing an online party for the company’s birthday. Everyone received a box of snacks with instructions: “Open at exactly 7 pm on camera.”
Your flatmate complains you’re on video calls all day and he hears every word. He says he now knows more about your project than his own.
A colleague five hours ahead is signing off and writes: “My day’s over, handing my stuff to you.” You have three hours left and enough of your own.
right: Ask to pick it up tomorrow

text: You shut the laptop at 6 pm, but half an hour later your hand reaches for it “just to check email.” Habit beats willpower.
A childhood friend visiting asks: “So what do you actually do at work?” You realise you spent the day on calls and can’t recall a single decision.
At Friday’s online quiz you know the answer, but your team captain — your manager — confidently picks the wrong one. Ten seconds left in the round.
In the evening you look around: cables everywhere, laptop on the sofa, notebook on the bed, headphones in the kitchen. Work has quietly spread into every room.
right: Deal with it at the weekend

text: The sales director, four hours behind you, is having a productive afternoon: at 9 pm your time he writes “Shall we discuss?”
After nine hours in headphones your ears are burning and your head still echoes “you’re on mute.” The last call is 30 minutes. Skip the headphones?
You tried working in timed sprints: 25 minutes on, 5 off. By evening you see you did 3 work sprints and 14 breaks.
Mom video-calls and sees the jungle of cables behind you. “Is that your job?” she asks, worried. She wants to come and help tidy up.
At an evening online quiz you’re asked colleagues’ surnames. You know all their pets’ names but not a single surname.
By evening your back aches and your neck only turns one way. You promised yourself a walk, but the sofa and a series are calling.
In the off-topic chat, colleagues are discussing how they cope with remote life. Someone admits he feels lonely. The chat goes quiet, waiting for a reaction.
At 11 pm an email from your manager arrives, flagged “High importance,” with one word: “Tomorrow.” Nothing else. Sleep suddenly seems unlikely.
The downstairs neighbour bangs on the radiator: your rolling chair has been squeaking across the laminate all day and he hears it all. In the evening he comes up to talk.
Your partner proposes a rule: no work talk in the flat after 7 pm. Tonight you have a call with the team on the other side of the world.
In the evening your child asks for the work laptop “to play for five minutes.” You remember it’s logged into the client database and a chat with your manager.
Online team building: a pasta masterclass. The chef on screen is already rolling dough, and you’ve just realised you have no flour, no eggs and no patience.
Friday, 6:30 pm. The manager wants to “wrap up the week.” He’s been showing slides for forty minutes, and you promised to collect a parcel before 7.
At stand-up everyone says what they did yesterday. You mostly fixed a printer nobody even needs at home and argued with the cat. What do you say?
At 9:00 sharp the drilling starts next door. You post in the building chat and find ten other remote workers with the same complaint and one revenge plan.
Dasha writes at 8:20: “I’m ill, but it’s fine, I’ll work from bed.” A minute later her task is reassigned to you “temporarily.”
The former office manager now runs “remote culture.” Today he wants everyone to raise their coffee mugs to the camera together at 9:00. You haven’t made coffee yet.
You wake to 80 emails sent overnight by colleagues across time zones. Every one says “urgent” or “ASAP.”
You bought a coffee machine to make home “feel like the office.” It’s so loud it carries on calls. Morning coffee or silence?
Your manager writes: “Morning! Got 5 minutes?” It’s the first time you’ve seen him online at 7:30. His boundaries have blurred too, apparently.
Your teenage son asks if he can go “remote” and skip school too. He says you’re setting the example: “You work from home, don’t you?”
You must now file a daily report of yesterday’s work. Writing about what you did takes longer than doing it.
The team lead DMs: “I notice you’re always off camera. Is everything OK?” Honestly, it’s just more comfortable. But the question sounds caring.
On a call with foreign partners, auto-captions translate your “let’s push the deadline” as something about “pushing the dead line into a drawer.” The partners look puzzled.
You discover the colleague you’ve chatted with for a year is actually two people job-sharing one role and one account.
left: Ask who you’re talking to now

text: Someone video-calls you unannounced: “Oh, I just wanted to ask by voice.” You’re in a ketchup-stained T-shirt and the camera turned on by itself.
right: Decline, call back in a minute

text: On the all-hands the director announces good news and asks for “a round of applause.” Everyone is muted, clapping silently into their cameras.
The client shares her screen and you spot a bookmark: “How to find a new contractor.” The call is about renewing your contract.
The product manager sends a link to a 40-page doc: “take a look before the call.” The call is in 15 minutes. The doc loads slowly.
right: Admit you didn’t get to it

text: You set a photo of your cat as your avatar. A week later new colleagues on a call are genuinely surprised you’re a human who can talk.
A client says mid-call: “One sec, I’ll step away for five minutes, don’t hang up.” Thirty minutes later his empty chair is still on screen; you have another urgent task.
Zhenya joins calls from his car, the shops, the pool. Today it’s a Ferris wheel. You can’t hear him, but he’s waving. You’re running the meeting.
Your daughter walks into frame in a dinosaur costume and roars just as the director asks your opinion on the budget. The camera sees everything.
The postman has a registered letter and needs your signature in person. You’re mid-call with a client discussing deadlines. He’s rung three times.
IT support asks for remote access to update your laptop. The cursor starts moving on its own while your report document is open.
Your messenger status got stuck on “At lunch” three days ago. Colleagues joke you never stop eating and post restaurant menus in chat.
The bank calls mid-meeting to offer a credit card. You decline. It calls again. And again. The phone buzzes right next to the mic.
A new chat appears: “Project X — working group.” An hour later come “Project X — working group (new)” and “Project X — important only.” Each says something different.
Third day eating lunch at your monitor while reading email. Today you finally sit by the window. Then a notification pops up: “Urgent: client edits.”
HR runs an online Secret Santa: send a gift by post to a colleague in another city. You’ve drawn someone you’ve never even seen on video.
The cat is yowling outside your “office” door again: you closed it for a call and he takes it personally. Thirty minutes left on the call.
At 8 pm the team lead posts “Great work today, team!” followed by “And one small thing for tonight.” The small thing is redoing a presentation.
Over a video call Grandma asks to see “where you work now.” You turn the camera to the sofa and the table. She looks sad: “And where does your boss sit?”
left: Show her the boss on video

text: You promised yourself an evening bike ride every day. Today the bike in the hall wears a sign saying “This is a coat rack” — your partner’s joke.
In the evening you scroll through old office photos: the shared table, a cake, colleagues in silly hats. Suddenly you want to message everyone.
For the first time the remote company needs someone to fly to a client meeting. Everyone looks at you: you have “the most decent jacket on video.”
The neighbour starts drum practice every night at 7. You used to get home at 8; now that’s when you call the regional offices.
You notice you averaged 11 hours a day this week. Nobody asked; the laptop was just always there. Will you change anything?
At 9:30 pm Roma DMs you a huge post about feeling everyone undervalues him. You’re on the sofa and almost relaxed.
Your partner made a candlelit dinner. You forgot about the 8 pm call with the team on the other side of the world. The laptop is already pinging.
At 9 pm a survey bot asks you to rate your “remote happiness” from 1 to 10. Under it, you notice anonymity is “partial.”
Colleagues invite you to an online game after work “for bonding.” You’ve never played, and your manager is already waiting in the squad.
Your partner says you muttered “you’re breaking up, say again” in your sleep. You’re dreaming of calls now. Tomorrow has eight more meetings.
You decided to work a week from the family dacha. This morning you learn the signal only reaches the shed roof, and your project review is at 9:30.
At the dacha the neighbour’s rooster crows every 20 minutes from 5 am. Today it made it onto the investor call recording three times.
You have a new manager you’ve never met in person. He asks for a “short bio” by 10 am “to get acquainted.” You’ve worked here three years.
A new Wi-Fi network appears this morning: “5th floor, stop calling at 7 am.” You live on the fifth and call at 7 am.
right: Move early calls to the kitchen

text: You’re having your flat renovated; the builders arrived at 8. The only quiet room is the bathroom. You have a key partner call at 9.
left: Take the call from the bathroom

text: Your coworking pass has doubled in price. The manager offers an “early bird” rate: cheaper, but only valid 7 to 11 am.
right: Go back to working from home

text: A colleague six hours ahead left you an overnight “handover”: 14 bullet points and one giant exclamation mark with no explanation.
You’ve been asked to onboard a new hire fully online. He sends 36 questions, starting with “so where’s the kitchen here?”
Your child’s school uses the same video platform as your work. You log in this morning and land in Year 4’s maths lesson.
On the morning call the host asks everyone to “turn cameras on so we can see faces.” You’re still wearing a sleep mask with cartoon eyes.
left: Keep the mask, make a joke

text: Yulia asks you to wake her every morning with a message because “remote life blurs my routine.” Today she hasn’t replied for half an hour.
You used to read on the metro on the way to the office. Now there’s no commute, and the book has sat on the nightstand for two months. Twenty minutes until work starts.
Leadership asks in an anonymous form: “Would you like to meet in a shared coworking space once a month?” Your vote will shape the whole team’s budget.
The laptop died overnight: someone unplugged the extension to charge the vacuum. Call in ten minutes, battery at 3%.
left: Sit on the floor by the socket

text: You notice nobody has replied to your team-chat messages for a week. Turns out an admin accidentally blocked you from posting. Nobody noticed you’d gone quiet.
right: Feel hurt and message the admin

text: A designer in another time zone needs logo approval by 8 am your time or “everything slips a day.” You see the message at 7:58.
The manager proposes an “experiment”: no calls before lunch. The first silent morning is unsettling: nobody needs anything. What do you do?
You’ve started morning yoga before work. The cat considers the mat his and lies on it the moment you go into downward dog.
At 8:40 your daughter realises you’re “home anyway” and wants a “healthy breakfast like in the adverts.” You have a board call at 9.
The online workshop splits everyone into breakout rooms of three. Your two roommates are silent with cameras off. Results are due in 10 minutes.
Your wireless mouse died and there are no spare batteries. You’re on the touchpad and the cursor has a mind of its own. A layout is due in an hour.
The CFO says the company is saving on rent, so “everyone gets a home office bonus.” But you must choose: desk or chair.
Seryozha suggests “body-doubling” over video: both silent, but visible to each other, “so we don’t get distracted.” He’s always crunching snacks.
Abseiling window cleaners are washing your tower block. One of them hangs right outside your window during a call, peering at your screen with interest.
The client added you to their company chat: 340 people, all typing at once, and nobody introduced you. Your question sinks in seconds.
Sales launched an online leaderboard of daily calls made. You were added by mistake — you’re an accountant. You’re dead last.
right: Make a few calls for fun

text: Your AI helper drafted a reply to a client. It’s polite, but instead of “Dear Peter” it says “Dear Peter, cat lover.”
Alya asks you to cover her call because “my child is sick at home.” It’s the third time this week, and your own report is on fire.
A neighbour turns up with a cake: “I see you’re home all day too, let’s be friends!” You have a call in three minutes.
The client is reviewing your work online. Two minutes of silence, just scrolling. The camera shows him frowning. You’re holding your breath.
A 12-person meeting where only two talk. The rest, judging by the sounds, are washing up, walking dogs and scooting. You’re asked for your view.
Friday online party: karaoke. The audio lag means everyone sings at different times. The host proudly picks you next.
A coworking neighbour suggests you start a startup together in the evenings. He says “you’re obviously bored at your job.” You are, a little.
Checking tomorrow’s calendar: calls at 7 am, 11 am, 3 pm, 7 pm and 11 pm — one per team time zone.
The dog has seen you home all day and doesn’t get why you won’t play. In the evening he brings every toy he owns and lays them round your chair.
A friend envies your remote life: “You’re basically free all day!” You’ve just finished a ten-hour day and want to tell her the truth.
Your work laptop needs three hours for a big update. Evening is ideal, but you promised a colleague you’d be online till 9.
Your family made a group chat and named it “Work matters” “since you answer work chats faster.” Now tasks land there: buy bread, collect your brother.
right: Ask for the normal family chat back

text: The company booked a 7 pm online museum tour “for personal growth.” The guide is passionate, but half the group has drifted off to their own stuff.
In the evening you realise you haven’t looked out the window all day. The sun has set and you never saw it. How long can this go on?
You’re moving to another team. Tonight your old team sends a 1,000-piece jigsaw made of screenshots from your calls together.
Online team building with pizza delivered to each home. The courier mixed up addresses and you got pineapple pizza, which you hate.
For the first time in a month you head out to work from a café. The scooter dies halfway, and the morning call is in 12 minutes.
Nina asks in the team chat: “Does anyone know if stand-up is on today or cancelled?” Nobody knows. The calendar link leads to an empty room.
Your uncle, staying with you, is up at six and by nine demands attention: “Are you going to sit in that box all day?” The box is your laptop.
You need to print and sign a document by 10 am. Your home printer only prints in pink because the other inks ran out.
Colleagues started a chat for posting morning step counts. With your 140 steps (bed–kitchen–desk) you’ve been last for a week.
At 8:05 the department head writes: “Cameras on all day today, we have an engagement audit.” You haven’t washed a single decent T-shirt.
You ordered groceries for 8 am, but the courier writes: “Arriving 9:15, be home.” You’re always home, but at 9:15 you’re presenting.
The team lead trials “async stand-ups”: everyone records a short video. You’re on your seventh take.
Your toddler has discovered the router’s lovely button and presses it every morning at 9:02. Stand-up has cut out three days running.
right: Give the kid a button of his own

text: The company invites everyone to a rented office for “meet-up day.” Your access card fails: the system lists you as “dismissed last year.”
On a call you finally see the new director — with a virtual background of palms and a sunset. He’s talking about “strict austerity.”
Vlad writes in capitals: “WHO TOUCHED THE PRESENTATION.” You did — you fixed one typo. He’s either furious or just hit Caps Lock.
The tracker marks your day “Low productivity: 47%” because you spent three hours thinking about a problem without touching the keyboard.
The cat knocks a glass of water onto your notebook of passwords and notes. The ink is running. You need to log into the client’s system in 20 minutes.
A new hire reacts 🙏 to every message from the boss. Colleagues have already given her a nickname in DMs and invite you to join in.
The manager caps all calls at 25 minutes. The very first one cuts off mid-sentence. No decision made.
You open a shared doc and see nine cursors with colleagues’ names on it. All editing the same paragraph. Your text disappears before your eyes.
right: Copy it out and edit privately

text: The moment you start talking to the client, the neighbour starts drilling. The client smiles: “Oh, renovating too? I get it.” You’re not.
The company launches mandatory online security training. The test can be retaken endlessly. A colleague DMs you all the answers.
The barista at the café you work from hints politely: “You’ve had one cup for four hours. There’s a queue for tables.” You have half a day left.
On the all-hands a colleague’s mic is open and his toddler is singing to all forty people. You’re co-host and can mute him.
Kirill sends you a message clearly meant for his mum: “OK, I’ll call after this boring meeting.” The meeting is yours.
You’re asked to “jump on a call” with a team you don’t know. You join; they’ve decided everything already and just want you to “be present.”
You went out for an hour with an auto-reply saying “Lunch.” You return to 14 replies saying “Enjoy your meal!” to your auto-reply, each awaiting a response.
Your call software has enabled “fun effects”: every time you cough, confetti explodes on screen. You have a slight cold.
Partners want a video invitation to their conference. Everyone else is busy and you’re the only one with a good camera at home.
At 8:15 pm the manager writes: “Can you take a quick look? Five minutes.” The file is 2 gigabytes and takes forty minutes to download.
In the evening the cat lies on the laptop and refuses to move. The warm lid is his new heating pad. You still wanted to send one email.
You’re planning a month working from somewhere warm. It’s five hours ahead, so the team’s evening calls would fall in your night.
Oleg posts a photo from a seaside walk: “Now this is remote work!” It’s 5:30 pm and you’re finishing his task.
The company bought tickets to an online concert for the team. It starts at 9 pm and HR will “take attendance.”
Your neighbour brings you a plate of pilaf: “Saw you working late again.” He wants to chat, and you have a call in 15 minutes.
right: Thank him and close the door

text: An evening notification: your salary is 15% lower — a “regional coefficient for remote staff.” You live exactly where you always have.
An online trainer at the evening workout shouts “Ten more push-ups!” Your camera is on and your manager, also in the class, can see you lying down.
You’re on holiday but “accidentally” brought the laptop. In the hotel in the evening an email arrives: “We know you’re on holiday, but…”
right: Lock the laptop in the safe

text: You went for an evening walk without your phone. Back 40 minutes later: 12 missed calls from your manager. The last message: “Never mind, sorted it.”
Marina writes: “Sorry it’s so late, my kid only just fell asleep and I need to discuss the report.” It’s 10:40 pm.
You open the fridge for the twentieth time today and realise remote work has turned into hourly snacking. It’s 9 pm.
In the evening the HR bot sends a “personal tip”: “You were online for 13 hours. Please rest.” Followed instantly by: “Don’t forget to file your report.”
The company VPN won’t connect this morning. Without it, no email, no task board. IT support opens at 10 am — in another city’s time zone.
The login code goes to your old phone, which is dead in a drawer. Its charger vanished in the last move. Work awaits.
Every morning at 8:30 Stas posts a cat picture captioned with the weekday. Today it says “Mon.” It’s Tuesday. You feel uneasy.
The clocks changed in your main client’s country. You find out when you join a call that started an hour ago.
Since going remote, your personal laptop became your work one. This morning your daughter needs it “for class” — her school has a remote day.
The internal “Remote News” newsletter sends “10 ways not to burn out” each morning. Today it features your photo captioned “Our hero of the month.”
Your desk is the kitchen table. At breakfast your laptop is surrounded by plates, crumbs and kids’ cereal. Call in five minutes.
A newcomer in another time zone joins stand-up an hour early every day and sits alone in the empty room for half an hour. He’s too shy to ask.
At 7 am the director wishes the whole company “Have a great day!” with a winking 😉. The chat explodes: some think it hints at layoffs.
Your laptop wakes up before you do: you’re asleep but it already told colleagues you’re online since 8. Status: active.
You started morning runs, but an 8:30 call means running with an earbud in and mic off. Someone asks you a question mid-stride.
Mom is staying for a week. Every morning she brings tea to your desk and sits beside you “to watch you work.” Sometimes she offers tips.
right: Ask her not to sit there

text: You decided to soundproof your study. The installer arrives at 8 promising to work “quiet as a mouse.” A mouse with a hammer drill.
left: Decamp to a café for the day

text: The team votes on where to hold an in-person meet-up: “resort,” “coworking” or “Misha’s dacha.” Misha has voted three times.
You ask a question and silence follows. Ten seconds later you realise everyone is waiting for you to finish — your audio simply dropped.
You ask the HR bot how to claim for your chair. It confidently sends 2019 rules, from when everyone worked in the office.
right: File it under the old rules

text: In your draft, accidentally shared with the whole department, a colleague comments: “Too emotional.” It was a letter to your mum; wrong folder.
An online auditor asks you to show on camera that no outsiders are in your workspace. You turn the camera: your flatmate in a bathrobe waves from the sofa.
You’re demoing to a client over video. At the big moment your laptop announces: “Restarting in 5 minutes to install updates.”
Nail, in another time zone, asks you to call a bank for him — it’s closed where he is but open where you are. It’s his personal business.
Leadership cut the office lunch budget but added a “remote wellbeing budget.” It can only be spent on meditation courses from one vendor.
The cat paws the door open and parades across the desk, tail up, in front of the camera during your board presentation. A board member laughs.
At the coworking space the person next to you keeps glancing at your screen. You’re handling confidential client data. He smiles and asks where you work.
A colleague going on holiday asks you to “keep an eye on chat” for urgent stuff. He’s in 23 chats and everything is urgent.
Mid-presentation you realise only you can see the slides. The audience sees your desktop wallpaper: cats in hats.
You message IT support. A bot replies: “Try turning it off and on.” You tried. The bot suggests it again, politely and relentlessly.
right: Just turn it off and on

text: Your brother also works remotely in the same flat. You’re both on calls at once, accidentally echoing each other’s lines. Your client is confused.
left: Divide the room with a wardrobe

text: The company holds an online send-off for someone leaving after ten years. Toasts are given. You barely know him, but it’s your turn to speak.
An evening newsletter: “The city office is open again for anyone who wants it, desks bookable a week ahead.” Do you want to go back, even once?
A colleague abroad suggests an evening language exchange: half an hour each teaching your native tongues. Useful, but it’s yet another call.
Your son asks to join your next call because “it’s fun and everyone laughs.” Today he eavesdropped on a meeting.
You enrolled in an online English course to understand foreign clients. Class is at 8 pm, which is exactly when you have a call with those clients.
right: Ask a colleague to stand in

text: Your neighbour’s husband drops by: “You know computers, you’re always home.” His printer is broken. Printers again.
A coworking neighbour invites everyone to “networking with pizza” at 7. For three weeks you haven’t talked to anyone except colleagues on a screen.
On Friday evening the manager sends a 12-minute video “instead of an email.” You’re in a taxi to a friend’s birthday.
The company pays for online fitness. In the evening class you see all of accounting in leggings on screen. Do you join in?
You’re scheduling a call across four time zones. The only slot that suits everyone is 11:30 pm for you. Everyone else is fine.
In the evening you notice your desk chair has worn a hole in the rug. A gift from relatives. It can still be saved.
Your teenager offers a side hustle: he’ll “sit in on your calls with the camera off.” He says he’s studied your voice and catchphrases.
In the evening chat colleagues debate whether “thanks” without an exclamation mark is rude. It reaches the manager, who reacts 👌.
In an online escape game you’re locked in a virtual room with the CFO. You must solve a riddle together to get out. He says nothing.
You bought a sit-stand desk. This morning it rose to maximum height and jammed. Call in 10 minutes, and the desk is at chin level.
You bought a ring light to look good on calls. Colleagues say you now have two glowing doughnuts in your eyes and look like an alien.
The new “smart” noise suppression removes your dog’s barking — and your voice when you speak softly. It’s early and you’re whispering; everyone’s asleep.
Your partner booked the only quiet room in the family calendar for the whole week: big project. You have one too.
The company sent every remote worker a houseplant “for morale” and asks for weekly photos. Yours is clearly dying.
Your company laptop was delivered to the neighbours by mistake. They’ve gone to their dacha for a week. You can’t work without it, and the manager wants a report.
The team’s “morning coffee photo” streak is at 99 days. You’re out of coffee, and everyone expects something special for day 100.
The smoke alarm’s battery is dying: it chirps loudly every 40 seconds. No spare battery of the right type. The morning client call is an hour long.
left: Take it down and stash it

text: On a call you say “remind me about the report,” and the smart speaker in the room answers loudly: “Reminder set. Would you like some relaxing music?”
Gosha starts every message with a string of smileys: “Hi :)))).” Today it’s “Hi :).” Just one. The team panics: is Gosha upset?
You worked on battery late last night and forgot to charge the laptop. It won’t turn on. The charger is in the car, and the car is at your partner’s work.
Your family has decided the living room is now a “shared open-plan.” In the mornings you work there, your child studies and Grandma does her exercises.
You forgot the out-of-office on Friday, and on Monday find 30 “are you there?” messages. Half from clients, half from a bot.
A newcomer asks to “shadow your workday”: keep a video link open all day and watch you work. He says he’ll learn faster.
The bank notifies you of a charge for a coworking space you used exactly once. The subscription auto-renewed for a year.
left: Call the bank and the space

text: You’re so cold this morning that you join stand-up wrapped head to toe in a blanket. Only your nose shows. The lead asks who that is.
The CEO video-calls you personally at 8:15. He doesn’t know you’re in dinosaur pyjamas, and your camera defaults to on.
Someone accidentally posted “Mum, buy bread” in the Announcements channel. It’s pinned, because the author is an admin.
A colleague sends a spreadsheet “please take a look.” It has 47 tabs, none clearly named. They want an answer by 3 pm.
A remote intern has been too scared to ask questions and has struggled silently with a task for three days. Today he writes: “Can I ask a dumb question?”
right: Send a link to the guide

text: Lera replies to a budget-cut announcement with a GIF of a dancing sloth. The manager reacts ❓.
The call recording went to the client in full — including 20 minutes after he left, when the team discussed his habit of being late.
right: Hope he doesn’t watch to the end

text: The cloud is full and won’t save your report. The biggest folder is yours: 40 GB of cat photos.
Background blur keeps swallowing your hands when you gesture. The client thinks you’re doing magic tricks and asks for an encore.
The manager reviews code live in front of the team. He opens yours and goes quiet. Then says: “Interesting…”
A freelance designer sends the mockup and the invoice at once. The mockup is wrong. The invoice is right.
HR launched an anonymous Q&A box for leadership. A glitch shows your name on your salary question during the all-hands.
The neighbour’s dog, home alone, has been howling for two hours. The owner is at work. You have her number, but your call starts in five minutes.
At a big online conference the moderator mixes you up with another speaker and introduces you as “an expert in quantum logistics.” You’re an accountant.
You see a colleague you’ve messaged for a year for the first time. His voice is nothing like you imagined. You giggle in the first minute.
You try a video lunch with a colleague, like the old canteen days. You both eat in silence, staring at the screen, awkwardness growing with each spoonful.
Your partner works in the next room and messages you: “Want some tea?” You’re on a call, but this chat is far more interesting.
The manager shares a team activity report: messages sent per person. You have the fewest, though you closed the most tasks.
HR sends a quiz: “What type of remote worker are you?” Result: “Lone wolf.” HR wants to discuss results on the team call.
You realise you’ve worn the same hoodie on camera for two weeks. A colleague in chat calls it “your corporate uniform.”
Your partner suggests a board game tonight. You’ve opened the task board three times “just to check.” He’s confiscated your phone.
Dina gives a video tour of her balcony office: desk, chair, fairy lights. You look at your laptop on the ironing board.
At the Friday social call everyone sips tea and discusses TV shows. You haven’t seen any — all your free time goes on work.
In the “Remote parents” chat they discuss working with kids at home. Someone proposes “chipping in for a shared video nanny.”
The cat is asleep on your desk chair. Twenty minutes of work left. Waking her is cruel; working standing up is tiring.
You’re about to go on holiday. The manager asks you to keep your phone on “in case of fire.” Your team has fires daily.
At bedtime your child asks: “What do you do? You just talk to the computer all day.” You stop and think.
You sent the report at 7:59 pm and shut the laptop. At 8:01: “Thanks! One tiny tweak.” The tiny tweak affects the whole spreadsheet.
HR runs “Remote Bingo.” Squares: “cat on camera,” “you’re on mute,” “someone eating.” You win by filling every square in one of your own calls.
Your dacha neighbour found out you work remotely and wants help with his online orders. He brings a bag of cucumbers “as payment.”
On an evening call the manager unexpectedly offers you a promotion — if you move to head office’s time zone.
You’re watching a series while rehearsing tomorrow’s presentation in your head. You’ve missed three episodes of plot. What now?
You’re working from a train on the way to family. The morning call coincides with a long tunnel: the connection drops every two minutes, mid-sentence.
You’re on a “workation” by the sea. Sand got into the keyboard and the letter “o” no longer types. A report on “turnover volumes” is due by lunch.
right: Ask a colleague to finish typing

text: You go to work in the library — quiet and free. Five minutes into a call the librarian hisses: “No talking in here.”
Your manager moved to the far side of the country and now starts work while you sleep. Every morning: 15 messages saying “hello??”
The new “smart framing” camera tracks the most active object. Today that’s the cat zooming round the room. You’re somewhere in the corner.
On the morning call, colleague Timofey forgets his video is on and brushes his teeth. The host hasn’t noticed. You have.
The postman delivers a paper invite to an online conference you’d totally forgotten. It’s today at 10 am, and you’re a speaker. It’s 9:20.
A neighbour walking his dog offers to take yours out in the mornings too, because “you’re always busy.” For free.
Each morning a bot asks “How are you feeling?” with five emoji options. Today you want a sixth that doesn’t exist: “like a wet sock.”
Your student sister is staying over and grabs the only socket by the desk first thing — she has online lectures too. Your laptop’s at 15%.
Colleagues post sunrise photos of their workspaces. Your view: the wall of the next building and somebody’s rug drying.
left: Post the rug, with a joke

text: A contract must be e-signed by 10 am. The USB key with your signature stayed in the office that closed three months ago.
right: Ask the client for more time

text: Arseny asks to swap on-call shifts: he wants a holiday, and you’d get the bank-holiday shift. He says: “You’re home anyway.”
While sharing your screen, a notification pops up: “Don’t forget your haircut at 3 pm.” The manager sees it.
right: Announce you’ll be out an hour

text: Bella writes “urgent!!!” and sends a link to a doc you can’t access. She’s gone into a two-hour call.
You decide to lie down for a 10-minute break. Ten minutes later you wake as someone calls your name on a call for the third time.
A client proposes an “online lunch”: everyone eats at home while discussing the contract. He has steak; you have yesterday’s pasta.
The space bar is sticking. Every chat message looks like: “Yes,agreed,willdo.”
Designers ask everyone for a photo of “what inspires you” for a team mood board. Everyone sends mountains and sea. You have a photo of your fridge.
On a call, someone off-screen at a colleague’s place says loudly: “Talking to your boring workmates again?” He goes red. Everyone heard.
left: Smooth it over with a joke

text: The company brings everyone together in person for the first time. You meet a colleague you’ve only chatted with for two years — she’s a head taller than you imagined.
The server crashed on your night shift. On a daytime call you’re asked to “share the experience” as a presentation by Friday.
Mid-presentation you get the hiccups. Every ten seconds you jump in frame. Thirty people politely pretend not to notice.
The company launched an internal podcast and invites you on to talk about “remote life.” Recording is today at 3 pm, no prep.
Your manager flags your task “Overdue,” though the deadline is 6 pm your time. In his time zone, it’s already passed.
The former office manager runs a “virtual kitchen”: a call to chat on your breaks. So far it’s just him, looking sad.
While you were on a call, your child ordered 14 tubs of slime from your account. The confirmation hit your work email, which your assistant can see.
The cat has learned to close the laptop with one paw. Every evening at 7:00 sharp he slams the lid. You’re no longer sure who’s in charge.
Colleagues sing you happy birthday over video in the evening, with lag. It becomes a six-part round.
The neighbour says your window is lit every night till 1 am. “What are you doing in there, working?” You are, actually.
You were issued a separate work phone. In the evening it’s in a drawer — but you can hear it buzzing through the drawer and the wall.
You put on a productivity podcast to relax. Ten minutes later you’re planning tomorrow. Work again.
At 9 pm Arkady posts a photo of his dinner: “Working since 7 with no lunch, here’s my reward.” It’s in the team chat, manager included.
Your partner suggests a weekend in the countryside with no internet. For the first time in six months you wonder if you can survive two days without notifications.
In the evening you order a new chair, desk and lamp. The basket equals a full year of your remote-work allowance.
HR wants everyone to film a greeting for the director’s anniversary. You film at 10 pm, the only kid-free time. Bad light, tired face.
You bought an online meditation course. The voice says: “Let go of all thoughts about work.” You remember you forgot to send the client an invoice.
Your company hoodie arrived three sizes too big. In the evening you wear it like a blanket. Turns out it’s comfy.
A coworking neighbour who saw your screen messages you that evening: “I’m hiring, come join me!” Better pay.
On a video call Mom asks when you last saw the sun. You honestly can’t remember. She silently sends you a link to a holiday deal.
You talk so much on calls that by evening you just want silence. Friends invite you to a board game night that’s all about talking.
Every morning Fyodor posts “Hi all!” in six chats. Today he posts in a seventh — your DM — and waits for a reply.
You bought a sunrise-simulating alarm. It lights up at 6:30 — straight into the eyes of your partner, whose calls start at 10.
The company set up an “Urgent” channel for emergencies. This morning it contains everything from “server down” to “who took my mug in 2019.”
A remote-working neighbour suggests morning coffee on the shared landing “like the office kitchen.” He’s already brought out two chairs and a table.
You must watch a 47-minute training video before 10 am. Double speed works, but the narrator sounds like a chipmunk — and there’s a test at the end.
right: Get up early and watch properly

text: You’re working from Grandma’s village. The signal only reaches the well. In the morning Grandma brings out a chair, a thermos and a wool blanket.
You’ve been made “chat morale officer.” Each morning you must post something uplifting. You haven’t uplifted yourself yet.
Your child is off sick. He’s on the sofa calling you every ten minutes to “just sit with me.” Morning tasks won’t wait.
At 8:50 the team lead cancels stand-up: “Async today, everyone write their update.” At 9:15 you’re the only one who has.
An app suggests an “eye exercise” every 20 minutes: look into the distance. Your distance is a wall. The app is insistent.
A coworking regular arrives when you do and takes “your” desk. Technically desks are shared. Practically, it’s yours.
On the call the manager praises “those who always have their camera on.” You stare at a row of black squares. One is you.
You accidentally switch on a virtual background of the old office. Colleagues get nostalgic and beg you to keep it forever, “like we’re together again.”
Vera shares her screen and hunts for a file. You see her desktop: 300 icons and a folder named “CV_new_final_really_final.”
An email arrives: “Urgent: confirm your password via this link,” signed by the CEO. The address looks odd. The CEO is in fact on holiday.
The call is booked until 2:30. At 2:29 the host says: “One last question.” You know that means another half hour.
You’re moderating a large online meeting. One participant won’t mute and is loudly explaining borscht to someone at home.
A neighbour kid’s drone hovers over the balcony where you work. It seems to be filming. You’re on a call with lawyers about a confidential contract.
Mitya DMs you a meme about the boss. A minute later: “Oops, not for you. Please delete.” The meme is genuinely funny.
You notice lunch has drifted to 4:30 pm and breakfast to noon. Your daily routine has dissolved into tasks.
In a meeting everyone agrees with a decision you think is a mistake. In the office you’d catch someone’s eye. Here, just squares.
Your landlord drops in unannounced to check the air conditioner. He walks into frame just as you say “everything’s under control.”
Your mentor abroad meets you monthly. Today he forgot and emails: “How about right now?” You’re about to start a call.
Your kitchen doubles as a meeting room. Your partner wants to cook lunch, but you have a 40-minute call. Fridge humming, soup on the hob.
You’ve spent an hour in chat on something a two-minute call would solve. Finally the other person writes: “Shall we just call?”
A colleague on holiday posts a beach photo in the team chat. Below it the manager: “By the way, where’s the report?” She’s silent. Answer for her?
The cat climbed into the new monitor’s box and won’t leave. The monitor won’t go back in, and IT is calling about returning the faulty unit.
right: Wait for the cat to leave

text: A colleague is running a company-wide online workshop. Five people turned up. He messages you: “Please bring some people.”
The manager wants all docs in “just one format.” Everyone interprets which one differently. The folder is chaos.
HR holds an online hobby fair: everyone shows off a pastime. Your only hobby for six months has been clearing your inbox.
In the evening you try watching a film from your desk chair, next to the laptop. Your body relaxes but your mind keeps working.
An online raffle for remote staff: the top prize is a week working from a rented country house. You win — and your manager is going too.
right: Gift the prize to a colleague

text: A friend suggests working from a warm city for a month. “You’re remote, who cares where?” The difference is three time zones.
You learn a colleague six hours behind stays up late every day to overlap with you. He’s never complained.
A friend asks you to refer him to your company: “I want to work from home in pyjamas too.” You doubt he knows what remote life is like.
You deleted the work messenger from your phone to rest in the evenings. At 8 pm a colleague calls your regular number: “Why aren’t you answering?”
At the company game night you’re paired with the quietest colleague. He turns out to be brilliant and cracks jokes for half an hour.
You promised to sort the drawer of cables from every old gadget. It’s 9 pm and you’ve found 12 identical chargers for nothing.
At 7:30 pm the manager writes: “Can you start early tomorrow, 7 am? Big call with the region.” You can refuse, but it’s awkward.
You hung fairy lights over your desk to make evenings cosy. Now colleagues think it’s a party every day and joke about it.
A student neighbour asks for help with his “project management” essay. You’ve managed projects for 8 years and are sick of it today.
The neighbours’ renovation crew blasts the radio at 8:30 every morning. You now know every morning song and the weather forecast by heart.
Ksyusha posts in the morning chat: “Working from the forest today!” The forest has no signal, it turns out. Her task is due by lunch.
The coworking space now books phone booths via an app. You booked 9 am, but the app says the booth is “taken” by your own account on another device.
right: Take the call in the car

text: You hung three clocks: your time, head office time and the client’s. This morning, after a clock change, all three are wrong.
An email from your manager this morning: “We need to talk. Free at 11?” Not a word more. Two hours to go.
Your partner joined a gym and gets up at 6. His alarm wakes you too. Your first call is at 10, but you’ve been up for three hours.
The company switches to a new call app. On the first morning nobody can find the mic button and everyone waves at their cameras.
You took your child out and joined the call from the playground. The swing squeaks so badly colleagues ask if you’re on a farm.
The manager goes on leave and makes you acting lead for a week. On the first morning you have 14 approval requests.
Your flatmate gets up earlier and takes the kitchen table — he works remotely too. He sets up three monitors and a coffee machine.
Every morning the manager records a one-minute video: “Good morning, team!” Today it features his guinea pig.
Your morning inbox has 20 “thanks,” “noted” and “ok” replies to a mailing list. Everyone hit reply-all. Your mailbox is full.
HR booked an 8 am online yoga instructor. You’re in downward dog when the cat sits on your back. Camera on.
Your son says this morning that it’s “careers day” at school and you need to talk to his class online at 10 am about what you do.
Leadership asks what time remote staff prefer to start. Options: 7, 8, 9. Everyone wants 10, which isn’t on the list.
The barista at your favourite café says “you work here more than I do” and offers a regulars’ discount if you arrive by 8.
During a screen share, Lyova’s browser shows a tab: “signs your boss is about to fire you.” He hasn’t noticed. You have.
A client in another time zone wants to call “at lunchtime.” You ask: whose lunchtime? He replies: “The normal one.” You’ve missed three calls this way.
You drop off a call and return a minute later. In that minute you were made responsible for the entire project.
Nonna asks in chat how to add a reaction. You explain, and she slaps a 💀 on the boss’s anniversary post. You message her again, fast.
You’re stuck in the lift with your laptop on the way back from the shop. There’s signal. Your presentation on the all-hands is in 10 minutes. The dispatcher says “about 40 minutes.”
You’re interviewing a candidate. Behind her a child shouts “Mum, I drew on the wallpaper!” She’s mortified. You need to continue graciously.
left: Joke that it happens to all

text: You leave a comment in a shared doc: “this is nonsense.” It was meant for a colleague’s DM. The client can see the doc.
Your work messenger account locked after five wrong passwords — the cat jumped on the keyboard. Only an admin in another city can unlock it.
Marketing is shooting “How we work remotely” and wants you “in your natural habitat.” Your natural habitat is pyjamas on the sofa.
A delivery robot carrying your lunch is stuck at the kerb outside. It blinks and posts “Please help me” in the app. Call in 7 minutes.
The manager asks in chat: “Can anyone cover my partner call in 10 minutes?” You’re not prepared, but nobody else answers.
The call app suggests: “It sounds noisy. Turn on noise suppression?” The only noise is your own voice. You’re alone.
The internal newsletter publishes a “most responsive colleagues” ranking by chat reply speed. You’re 87th of 90. A bot is above you.
Your partner suggests playing “office”: you both leave the flat, walk around, then “come home from work.” Weird, but you’re sick of these walls.
At 9 pm Sveta writes: “Thanks for saving me today!” You don’t recall how, but it’s nice.
You planned a sauna night with friends. At 6 pm the manager writes: “Need the spreadsheet access, and you’re the only one who has it.”
Dinner is cooking while you’re on a call. The smell of fried onions fills the flat and you realise you’ve missed a key part thinking about food.
In the evening the manager writes “Got an idea!” and sends seven voice notes. The last says: “anyway, we’ll discuss tomorrow.”
Your child’s party is tonight and you’re asked to be the “live entertainer” for online guests. After nine hours of calls, you doubt you can smile at a camera again.
A neighbour learns you work from home and offers you his food-blog dishes every evening. Free and tasty, but you must write a review.
HR runs an evening online game: “Draw a colleague.” You get the manager, and you draw live.
You can’t sleep: the client conversation keeps replaying. The phone is right there, and your hand reaches to send him “one more thought.”
You’re on holiday, but social media shows colleagues complaining about a broken server. You know a five-minute fix.
At 10 pm Grisha sends a funny meme about calls. You react 😂 and he instantly replies: “Oh, since you’re up…”
The company magazine wants to interview you about “work-life balance.” The only free slot is 9 pm.
You run in the evenings and dictate voice replies to colleagues on the go: “Yes… huff… will do… huff… tomorrow…” Colleagues are worried.
At 7:45 Yana sends a huge wall of ideas written overnight. It ends: “What do you think? Be honest.” Some ideas are brilliant, some bizarre.
Your windowsill office is flooded with morning sun: the screen is unreadable and you’re sharing a spreadsheet. The curtains are in the wash.
left: Hang a blanket over the window

text: You booked a key morning call, but half the team is in a region with a local holiday today. Three people came — none of the ones you needed.
The dog slipped his lead on the morning walk and chased a pigeon. Your presentation is in 7 minutes. He’s at the far end of the park, delighted.
You’re out of coffee pods and the shop opens at 10. Your call is at 9, and without coffee you speak in monosyllables.
At 8:00 the boss writes: “No calls today! Enjoy the focus.” At 8:05: “Except one.” At 8:07: “And a couple of small ones.”
A colleague two hours ahead is already at lunch when you wake up. She writes: “Where are you? I’ve been sorting this alone for half a day.”
The company sent everyone “coffee money for remote staff” via a new service. To claim it, install an app and complete a face scan.
Your aunt calls at 9:01 and wonders why you answered so formally: “Speaking.” You’re at stand-up and accidentally patched her into the call.
Borya books calls at 8 am and is always late himself. Today at 8:20 he writes: “5 minutes away.”
Your study doubles as the kids’ room. On the wall behind you hangs your child’s drawing: you with a giant head, titled “On a call again.” The camera sees it.
The team now rotates stand-up hosts weekly. It’s Monday and you’ve only just seen that this week it’s you. Four minutes to go.
A client five hours ahead wants a call “at the start of your day so I make it before the end of mine.” That’s 7 am.
The water-cooler supplier from the old office has delivered a 19-litre bottle to your home. He believes you are the office now and wants a signature.
Grandma saw your manager on video and now asks every morning: “How’s your boss, eating well?” Today she wants to send him pastries.
A wheel snapped off your desk chair this morning; it lists to the left. On calls you slowly slide out of frame.
Tikhon only sends scheduled messages at 23:59, 12:00 and 6:00. At noon today a question arrived whose answer was needed yesterday.
A colleague livestreams “cook with me” in the team chat at lunch, chopping onions and talking about the project. Suddenly everyone’s watching.
HR wants photos of your documents “on a plain background.” The only plain thing at home is the cat. A white cat.
Your partner’s call in the next room is so loud your client asks: “Who’s that talking about the quarterly plan?” You work for different companies.
right: Ask your partner to lower it

text: The manager recorded a 40-minute video guide. Half of it is him hunting for a tab. You need one number from it.
A window repairman has arrived, but you’re on a call. He waits in the hall and sighs loudly every 30 seconds.
Zoya sends you a voice note, clearly crying over client edits. In 10 minutes she’s due to present on the team call.
You post “Back soon” and go to lunch. You return an hour later to 30 messages: “where are you?” and “soon yet?”
Your mic now drops every other word. You say “We will not miss the deadline,” and they hear “We will miss the deadline.”
The cat demands food with loud yowls during a call. The bowl is empty, and colleagues ask whether everyone at your place is alive.
The company is voting online on a new product name. “Product 2.0” is in the lead. Your creative option is dead last.
You’re invited to an external online interview about your company. PR wants you to sound “natural” — from a 20-page script.
Your partner’s guest asks for the Wi-Fi password. It’s “IHateCalls2024.” Your partner looks at you.
The coworking space is having a “silent day” — no calls. But you have an important call, and all booths are taped shut.
On the wrap-up call the manager thanks the team but doesn’t name you, though you did most of the work. Everyone claps with emoji.
Colleagues on the other side of the world invite you to their “morning coffee” video chat. It’s 11 pm for you. They ask so sincerely that saying no feels awkward.
You decided to hit inbox zero by evening. Two hours later: 0 unread, but 14 new tasks you assigned yourself.
A friend’s birthday at a café. Mid-evening you catch yourself checking the work chat in the bathroom.
Gena writes in the evening: “Between us — I’m handing in my notice. Don’t tell anyone.” Tomorrow is the quarterly planning call with the manager.
right: Urge Gena to tell him himself

text: Your sister video-calls and spots the planning board behind you. “You have a project board at home?” You nod. She’s horrified.
Sunday evening. You’re watching a film, but Monday’s eight calls won’t leave your head. The laptop’s on the next chair.
In an evening online board game a glitch shows you everyone’s cards, the manager’s included. The prize is an HR chocolate bar.
The downstairs neighbours are partying till midnight. You have a 7 am call tomorrow with another time zone. You’re in bed above a karaoke night.
Friday, 6 pm. Someone writes: “Let’s not log off yet — video hangout?” Fifteen people join, the manager included.
Overnight the robot vacuum chewed through your laptop charger cable. Big call tomorrow. A replacement costs half a chair.
right: Ask a colleague to lend one

text: Your partner proposes a screen detox: all gadgets away for three hours. Your hand twitches towards your phone involuntarily.
At 7:30 pm Alina writes: “I’m lonely working remotely, can we just call and chat?” You’re tired of voices, but she clearly needs it.
In the evening someone proposes a challenge: a month with no messages after 7 pm. The manager hasn’t replied yet.
An evening courier brings a huge box: the company sent everyone a “cosy evening kit.” Inside: a blanket, candles and… a year-long work planner.
You bought dumbbells for stretching between calls. Tonight you notice they’ve been paperweights for a month.
Petya writes: “My internet was down all day, can you send my report tonight?” You saw his stories from the park this afternoon.
The neighbour across the landing invites you to his birthday. You haven’t socialised in person for so long you’ve forgotten how to talk without a mute button.
The team’s online film night: everyone presses play together and chats. The manager picked it: a three-hour drama about accounting.
Evening announcement: from Monday everyone meets in person once a week. There’s no office, so it’ll be in a café.
You installed a screen-time app. Tonight it shows 14 hours and politely asks: “Is everything OK?”
A runner neighbour suggests evening jogs together: “You sit all day.” He runs 10 km; you max out at the fridge.
At 8 pm the team lead writes: “I need your feedback on the new hire by morning.” You’ve seen him once, on a call, camera off.
Your daughter wants to learn to make slides “like you do at work.” You’re sick of slides, but she’s giving you that look.
After ten calls you catch yourself talking to the cat like a meeting: “Sorry, you’re on mute, can you repeat?”
Varya sends you her drawing “you on a call”: in pyjamas with a cat on your head. She wants to share it with the team.
right: Ask her to keep it private

text: You ran the wash at 9 pm so it won’t be loud on calls. At 11 pm it starts spinning and the neighbour bangs on the pipes.
The company is holding an online exhibition of employees’ children’s drawings. Your kid drew you at the laptop, titled “Always working.”
Oleg livestreams his evening fishing trip for the team. Five people watch him sit by the river for an hour and a half.
Your partner says you keep nodding at dinner like it’s a call, murmuring “yes, yes, agreed.” He just wants to talk.
left: Put the phone down and talk

text: In the evening you find your old office pass. In the photo you’re smiling. That was before three years of remote work. You want to change something.
right: Stick the pass on the fridge

text: The company wants time logged per task. A third of your day went on “answering where a file is.”
First restaurant in six months. The waiter asks something and you reflexively reply: “Yes, I can hear you fine, go ahead.”
Danya writes: “Could I work at your place sometimes? It’s noisy at mine.” He lives three streets away.
Your auto-reply says “I reply 9 to 6,” but at 10 pm the manager emails: “I know about your auto-reply, but…”
At the company’s online quest you solve the riddle, but everyone has left. It’s just you and the host. He asks whether to continue.
A coworking neighbour messages: “Lunch together tomorrow?” You barely know him, but you’re free at lunchtime tomorrow.
The room is stuffy, so you open the window. In rush tram noise and horns. Closed, it’s stuffy and sleepy; open, the client asks you to repeat every sentence.
The courier brings a work monitor — a 49-inch one, due to a warehouse error. It takes up the whole desk and half the room.
In the morning Rustam sends 8 screenshots without a word. Spreadsheets of some kind. He’s now in a call.
The neighbour’s dog barks at the postman every morning at 9. The postman comes every morning at 9. Your stand-up is at 9.
IT sent a new work laptop. Setup takes “just 3 hours.” The old one must be returned by noon today. You’re still in pyjamas.
Your calendar synced with your personal one: during a screen share a reminder pops up: “Buy socks for the cat.” Everyone sees.
A new manager’s first day. At 7 am she writes: “What’s everyone’s favourite time for calls?” The poll is open.
An online trainer runs company morning workouts. You volunteered. A week later you’re held up as an example, and now you can’t back out.
A friend joined your company remotely and wants “video lunch together every day.” You like quiet lunches.
You’re invited to an 8 am online investor meeting. The invite says “Dress code: business.” Nobody sees below the desk, but the top must be sharp.
Mom calls at 8:20 asking why you sounded sad in your voice note. You sent it at 11 pm last night after three calls.
The cat crawled into the desk drawer and fell asleep on your papers. You need one right now — the signed contract.
Anya from another department asks: “Can I send you my tasks every day so you keep me on track? It helps.” You’re not her manager.
You’re on a client call when the intercom buzzes: neighbours with a pie. It smells so good you lose your train of thought.
right: Ask them to come back later

text: Lyosha wants to “keep it office-like” and DMs you “Coffee?” every hour. It’s a joke — virtual coffee — but it distracts you.
The company introduces “core hours,” 11 to 3, when everyone must be online. You’re a lark: done by 11, fading by 3.
No hot water this morning, and a video call in 20 minutes. No time to wash your hair; yesterday’s hairdo looks exhausted.
You’re moving flats mid-week. This morning the movers carry out the desk — with your laptop on it, mid-stand-up.
A blizzard overnight; the whole district is offline. The teenager next door knocks: “Yours too? I’ve got an online test!”
right: Head into town with the laptop

text: Your child has an online lesson at 9, you have a call at 9. Bandwidth covers one video stream. Who switches off?
At 6:40 an investor replies to yesterday’s report with a single 🤔. Nothing else. The call with him is three hours away.
You’re working from a mountain hotel. The only signal is at a lookout 200 metres uphill. Stand-up at 9.
You’re working from a hotel. At 9:05, as your call starts, housekeeping knocks: “Cleaning!” The Do Not Disturb sign fell off.
right: Ask her to come back later

text: You dash off an important email to a client and hit send. Only then do you notice the keyboard layout was wrong: the email is gibberish.
Every Tuesday at 9 the rubbish truck empties the bins right under your window. It’s Tuesday, and you’re meeting a new client for the first time.
A pigeon has taken to visiting your balcony office. Today it perches on the laptop and peers into the camera during stand-up.
The company announces a four-day-week trial. Catch: Friday’s work gets spread over Monday to Thursday.
The meeting invite came in UTC. You added three hours; your colleague subtracted. It’s 9 and you’re each alone in empty rooms.
The manager scheduled emails for 9 am so as not to disturb evenings. A glitch delivered all 40 at 4 am.
The flat’s cold, so you work hugging the laptop like a hot-water bottle. Its fan blows warm air. A heavy task keeps it toasty.
left: Take on a second heavy task
right: Turn on the heater and relax

text: This morning the manager writes: “Help me run 6 online interviews today. All before lunch.” You have two days of your own work.
You’re hosting a 300-person webinar. Two minutes in, someone asks “when’s the break?” Ten minutes later everyone’s asking.
A colleague reacts 🙃 to your chat joke. Laughter, sarcasm or “oh please”? The joke was about his project.
The manager proposes testing an AI avatar that “attends” dull calls for you and nods. Tempting, but odd.
The chat-summary bot boiled a two-hour argument down to: “Discussed. Nobody agrees.” The manager wants details.
right: Forward the bot summary as is

text: The courier left lunch at your door; a minute later it was gone. The stairwell camera shows the neighbours’ cat dragging it off. In the bag.
Your calendar shows “Nap” from 2 to 3 pm. Colleagues book over it because “it’s not work.”
Your performance review is on video. The manager reads peer feedback. One says: “Good when the camera’s on.”
You’re asking for a raise on a call. At the crucial moment your video freezes mid-word, mouth open. Audio’s gone.
A book on the shelf behind you reads “How to Quit Gracefully.” A friend’s joke gift. The manager notices it on the call.
The neighbour’s cat walked along the ledge and in through your window. You’re on a call and he’s settled on the keyboard. Not yours, but very confident.
right: Keep him till the call ends

text: Your child’s online teacher asks for “a grown-up to come over.” You’re on a call with leadership.
You and a colleague draft a client email in a shared doc. She softens every sentence: “Urgent” becomes “Whenever convenient, perhaps.”
You’re put in charge of planning the team’s in-person meet-up. Fifteen people from five cities, budget fit for one dinner. Wishes are pouring in.
Your project is being discussed in a chat you weren’t added to. A colleague tips you off with a screenshot.
Your new webcam has a privacy shutter and you forgot to open it. For five minutes you wondered why everyone said “we can’t see you.”
The lift is broken and your new 40 kg desk has arrived. The courier won’t go past the entrance. Calls from 2 to 6.
A colleague posts a screenshot of your private chat in the team channel to “confirm what we agreed.” It also includes chat about your dog.
Auto-translate rendered your “I’m on a call” for a foreign colleague as “I’m in a bell tower.” He asks how the view is.
You’re demoing a prototype to a client over video. Off screen your child shouts: “That’s my colouring book!” It does look similar.
Groceries are due 7–9 pm. At 7 you have the quarterly review call with your manager. The doorbell is inevitable.
You downed a fourth coffee at 6 pm to survive the last call. At 11 pm you’re wired and ready to rewrite the whole project.
A coworking neighbour suggests evening English classes together: “Remote workers need to widen their circle.”
Your brother is visiting for a week and asks what time you’ll finish work. You don’t know. You never know.
You ordered an “office chair.” What arrived is a CEO throne: huge, leather and creaky.
A colleague plays guitar and hosts an online gig for the team on Friday night. He sings about deadlines. Five people came.
A colleague you’ve worked with on video for two years is passing through your city and asks to crash on your sofa.
Your daughter wants you to video-call her class tonight and explain “remote work.” You’re not sure you know any more.
At the end of a late call the manager says: “Right, you’re free to go.” But he doesn’t end it, and everyone waits to see who leaves first.
Friday, 8 pm. You’re with friends, and a heated thread is running in the work chat — you can see the notifications. You’re mentioned.
In the evening Galya sends you a job ad elsewhere: “I think it suits you. You work too well for us.”
Your partner suggests a “quiet hour” at home: no talking from 9 to 10 pm. After a day of calls, you’re almost relieved.
You’ve been added to your university alumni chat. Everyone shares career triumphs. You have a new ring light and a cat.
