left: Share the light and the cat

text: You’ve been put in charge of the team’s morning digest. Every day before 9 you must beg everyone for a line. Half are still asleep.
right: Write it from what you have

text: Every morning Tamara sends a seven-minute voice note “daily plan overview.” Today she accidentally sent it to the client.
This morning you’ve lost access to every work system. IT says: “You were deactivated as a leaver by mistake.” You haven’t left.
You used to hear podcasts on the metro; now you listen while washing up at 8. Today’s episode: “How remote work destroys teams.”
left: Share it in the team chat

text: Monday, 8:50. The chat says: “Everyone read the doc I sent on Saturday?” Nobody did — except you.
You switch the camera on and find the virtual background your kid set last night: outer space, with you in an astronaut helmet.
Today you’re on the support rota, answering client chats from 8. At 7:58 there are already 23 questions.
You commute to the coworking space by train. This morning yours is cancelled; the next is in an hour. Your meeting there is at 10.
An automated email: “You haven’t logged in for 30 days; your account will be deleted.” You log in daily. Deletion is at 10 am.
The team lead wants anonymous 1–10 ratings of colleagues’ “engagement on calls.” You know Misha’s mic is broken.
The call app added a “suggest a stretch” button. Someone hit it in the director’s meeting. Everyone is now waving their arms.
A courier brought documents to sign by 9 am and is waiting. It’s a 30-page contract. He leaves in 15 minutes.
right: Ask him to come back later

text: A decorator arrives to wallpaper your workroom. He needs everything out, desk included. You have 10 minutes between calls.
left: Move the desk to the bathroom

text: A colleague offers to install a program that “jiggles the mouse to keep you green.” He says everyone does it.
You blocked “Focus time, do not disturb.” Five minutes later the manager writes: “I know you’re focusing, but super quick…”
You’re presenting the product online to a client. His cat walks over the keyboard and accidentally clicks “Buy.” He doesn’t notice.
Everyone talks at once because of varying lag. It’s a chorus: “I think… I believe… Can I just…” You’re chairing.
Mark is sure you’re in the same time zone. Every day he writes “let’s talk in 5,” and every time it’s your evening.
The company launches an internal merch store for points. A year of remote work earned you exactly one mug and half a sticker.
The host force-muted you “for background noise.” Now someone asks you a question and you can’t unmute, so you wave frantically.
You lunch on the balcony and forget the laptop is still on a muted call. Colleagues stare at your empty chair for 20 minutes.
An unknown number calls: “Hi, I’m your new colleague from procurement. Can I ask something?” She’s calling your personal phone.
right: Ask her to use the chat

text: Vanya posts a photo of his project whiteboard. Also visible: a list titled “Who annoys me.” You’re third.
Your first e-signature. The app asks you to “draw your signature with the mouse.” It comes out looking like a hedgehog.
The company switches task systems. Old tasks will “migrate automatically.” Only titles migrated. No descriptions.
right: Wait for IT to fix it

text: Yura’s talking on mute again. Two minutes of wild gesturing. You can lip-read he’s cursing the system.
Your landlady learns you work from home and wants to raise the rent “for wear and tear.” She says you “sit there all day wearing everything out.”
HR runs an online debate: “Office vs. Remote.” You’re on team Office. You haven’t been in one for two years.
A colleague in another city asks you to order a cake for her mum, who lives in your city. She’ll transfer the money “tonight.”
You notice your email signature has said “Sent from my iron” for two months. Your kid’s joke.
A neighbour drops by proposing a shared Wi-Fi network for the floor to save money. He wants you as admin.
You find a note on your desk from your partner: “Work ended 2 hours ago. Dinner’s getting cold. So am I.” You’re on a call.
Olya writes: “I was on calls all day and did zero actual work. You too?” You too — but there’s still the evening.
The company’s online sports club runs a steps competition. Your team is last, and the captain asks everyone to walk 5,000 more tonight.
You enrolled in evening online courses to change careers. Mid-lesson the manager messages: “Where are you?”
You read your child a story and he asks: “Do the voice of your boss on calls.” You’re very good at it.
A client emails thanks in the evening and copies your manager, who instantly replies: “Great! What’s next?”
A colleague seven hours behind gets busy just as you go to bed. Your phone pings all night.
Friends at a café. Someone asks where you work. You start answering like a meeting: “OK, quick overview…”
It’s the last day of a colleague you worked with for three years but never met. He suggests meeting in person tonight.
A friend’s mum asks you to set up video calls with her grandkids. “You’re the call expert.” You just sit in calls.
The company introduces a weekly “wellbeing report.” One question: “How many times did you leave the house this week?” Answer: twice, for bread.
At the online residents’ meeting you’re made secretary because “you’re always at the computer.” They’re debating the stairwell colour.
The manager calls at 9 pm, not about work: he asks how you are. He says he’s worn out and just wanted to talk.
You’re flying to family and working from the departure lounge. The morning call coincides with boarding announcements every 30 seconds.
You’re given a new project with a team across five cities. First morning: nobody knows who owns what. Everyone looks at you.
Residents set up a “Remote workers of entrance 3” chat to coordinate noise. They pick you as admin because you “seem organised.”
The cloud folder synced wrongly overnight: your report is a three-week-old version. The manager wants it by 10.
Every morning Dima posts a running photo: “Who’s joining tomorrow?” Nobody has ever said yes.
At 7:30 a courier calls: “I’m at your office door, nobody’s answering.” It’s the old office address; the parcel is for you.
You installed a “focus mode” app that blocks everything but the editor until noon. At 10 the manager rings your phone: “Where are you?”
right: Explain and go back to focus

text: Accounting says the internet allowance now only goes to those with cameras on in every call. A bot will check.
The new team lead introduces “morning gratitude”: everyone thanks someone at stand-up. You haven’t interacted with anyone all week.
A colleague four hours ahead asks you to “be reachable from 6 am” for her big client. Just one day, she promises.
The cat is asleep on your mouse. Soft and warm, and there’s no getting it out without waking him. Work starts in five minutes.
A colleague who lives nearby suggests a morning café coffee “as if we were going to work.” You haven’t seen colleagues in person for ages.
The keyboard batteries died, so you pinch them from the TV remote. Now your partner can’t change the channel and is giving you a look.
A client invites you to a real restaurant lunch. You haven’t worn proper shoes in two years and can’t remember where they are.
A colleague shares his screen and you spot the careers page of a company he seems to be leaving for. In an hour you’re co-presenting a project with him.
You’re doing a mandatory online course. Every 5 minutes it asks “Are you still there?” You click on autopilot.
You mean to DM a colleague “I’m so fed up with this project” but post it in the project chat. The manager is typing…
You’re training a newcomer by video. He nods and says “got it” to everything. An hour later his question proves he got nothing.
A client video-calls unannounced. You’re eating soup, spoon in hand, mouth full, and the camera turns on automatically.
You get up to stretch and head to the kitchen. On the way: the cat, your partner with a question, a courier and a call from school. Back 40 minutes later.
The company cancelled its paid video-call plan. Calls now cut off every 40 minutes. Your meeting runs 90.
Ira writes: “Does anyone know how to turn off the beach background? I’m at Grandma’s 80th birthday.” She needs help fast.
While sharing your screen you accidentally open the chat where you and a colleague are picking the manager’s birthday gift. He’s on the call.
A colleague suggests a five-minute team stretch on video every day at 2. The manager approves but never attends.
The deadline is 6 pm client time. You’re not sure which time zone the client is in. It’s 3 pm your time and you’re nearly done.
The courier asks: “You’re home all day? Can I leave the neighbours’ parcels with you?” He’s serious.
The boss asks on the call: “Who’s for moving the deadline?” Silence. Yours is the only camera on. He’s looking at you.
The manager wants “three top achievements” at day’s end. Today’s top one: you didn’t fall asleep on the 4 pm call.
A friend invites you to the cinema tonight. As you leave, you notice you’re still in pyjama bottoms with a business shirt from your calls.
The flat is unusually quiet tonight — your partner’s away. You realise you only spoke to the smart speaker and your manager today.
You’re invited to an online “Remote Leaders” club. Forty people on video explain how they wake at 5 am.
The musician next door knocks: “You’re home all day, listen to my new song, I need an honest opinion.” It’s a long song.
You’re planning leave, but every week in the team calendar has a “key milestone.” The manager says: “Pick any.”
A late call with a team on the other side of the country. It’s their morning and they’re perky; you can barely keep your eyes open.
HR announces “Best home workspace.” The winner gets a new chair. Your desk is an ironing board with a cushion.
Your son asks if friends can come over tomorrow, “since you’re home anyway.” Tomorrow you have a board call.
Slava writes at 10:30 pm: “Up? I’ve figured out how to simplify our entire process.” It sounds brilliant, but it’s 10:30.
right: Ask him to write it up

text: The 8 pm online workout is your only one this week. At 7:55 someone books a “super short” call. The trainer’s waiting.
Playing a video game tonight, you see your manager online in the friends list. He sees you too. You left early today “on an errand.”
Your partner changed the Wi-Fi password overnight “for security” and left for work with the phone it’s saved on. Your call is at 9.
The team lead brags: “Our stand-up takes exactly 10 minutes!” Today it takes 47 because someone started on their holiday.
You work by the window; across the courtyard a neighbour is on calls too. You wave every morning. Today he’s waving frantically.
At 8 am colleagues send a video for your work anniversary, which you’d forgotten. Everyone’s in paper party hats.
Every morning a bot sends you yesterday’s undone tasks. The list has grown for two weeks.
The CEO started a morning livestream, “Coffee with the CEO”: 30 minutes of sipping and answering questions. Nobody asks any. He looks sad.
You find out a colleague juggles two remote jobs. This morning he asks you to answer for him on a call “while I’m on the other one.”
Your child set an alarm on your phone “for school” but got it wrong: it rings at 6 with a cartoon tune. You’re up.
The team agreed to meet monthly at a coworking space. Today’s the day, but only you and the team lead showed. Everyone else is on video.
In a poll “Which day suits you for meetings?” everyone picks “none.” The manager schedules them daily, “since there’s no preference.”
The building management heard you’re “always home” and asks you to let plumbers and electricians in all week. There are 120 flats.
Tanya writes: “Can I send you a ‘drink water’ sticker every morning?” Sweet, but you already have four such bots.
You booked an online doctor’s appointment for 9:30. The manager then schedules an emergency call at 9:30.
At a 2,000-person online conference you post a question. The moderator reads it out with your name — typo included: “How to increase porfit?”
A colleague posted a report with your numbers under his name. He seems to have just forgotten to credit you.
You’re working on the balcony and a gust blows your printouts into the courtyard. One is the client’s annual strategy.
Census takers ring the doorbell. You’re on a call, but they very politely ask for “just five minutes.”
right: Ask them to come back tonight

text: A communication trainer pairs everyone up and asks you to “look into each other’s eyes for 60 seconds.” Your partner is the CFO.
Your food courier is stuck in the lift and video-calls you for “moral support.” You’re in a meeting.
You accidentally reacted 😂 to “I regret to announce I’m leaving the company.” The colleague is silent. The chat is silent.
A freelancer you hired vanished for two days. Today he delivers with: “No internet on my fishing trip.” The work is excellent.
A video meeting has run two hours. You stand to get water and both legs are numb. The host says: “Literally five more minutes.”
Your daughter asks to print her essay on your work printer. It spits out your quarterly report by mistake. Five copies.
left: Give them to her as scrap

text: The manager accidentally enables a “sad puppy” filter. He can’t turn it off and runs the whole cost-cutting meeting as a puppy.
The coworking space has made the whole floor a “silent zone.” Talking only in booths, which cost extra. Your call is in 15 minutes.
Security runs a “surprise workspace video check.” They call and ask you to show you’re alone in the room. You’re in the bathroom.
The plumber next door offers a trade: he fixes your tap, you set up video calls with his daughter. Tonight.
right: Put it off till the weekend

text: End of quarter. The manager asks the team to work Saturday, “just half a day, it’s remote, no commute.”
The company hosts an evening online book club. The book is one you didn’t finish. The moderator asks your opinion.
The company sent you a gift — a smart speaker. In the evening it offers to “connect to your work calendar for convenience.”
The kids are fighting over the tablet in the evening while you’re on a call with the regional team. Their shouting carries clearly.
right: Shut the door and carry on

text: In the evening Zhenya sends screenshots of his new flat: “Moved — I’ve got a study now!” You’re happy for him, and a bit jealous.
You post “Good night, all!” in the work chat and it springs to life: half the team is still working and asks where a file is.
You finished an online course and got a certificate. The manager wants you to run a team workshop on it. Unpaid, in the evening.
In the evening the cat knocks your “Employee of the Year” award off the shelf. It shatters. Your only proof of office life.
right: Bin it and joke in chat

text: In the evening you’re asked to vote for “colleague of the year.” You personally know three people out of a hundred.
You’re doing evening DIY to build a home office. A neighbour knocks: it’s 10 pm and he has a 6 am call.
In winter it’s still dark at 9. On camera you look like a protected witness in a documentary. The lamp is being repaired.
Your first word of the day is at the 9:05 stand-up. You sound like a pirate. Colleagues ask if you’ve caught a cold.
Katya posts her minute-by-minute daily schedule “in case it helps.” The manager asks everyone to do the same by lunch.
right: Joke that my day is chaos

text: Documents arrive by drone on your balcony. It hovers until you tap a button in the app. The app won’t load.
The 9 am call was moved to 8, announced in the team chat at 7:55. You saw it at 8:10. Everyone’s waiting for your update.
You’re working from the dacha. At 8 the neighbour starts a petrol strimmer, audible on every call till lunch.
HR wants a 30-second “video intro” for newcomers. You’ve stumbled through 12 takes of “I own cross-functional synergy.”
Your favourite morning café, where you work, is closing for good. The barista knows your order and your Wi-Fi password.
You’re two minutes late because you couldn’t find the link. The host says: “Finally, we’re all here!” Everyone looks at you.
Alya asks to swap leave slots — she has a friend’s wedding. Your holiday would shift by a month, and tickets are bought.
The laptop has lived on the kitchen table for a month while the study desk you bought is buried in stuff. Morning — time for change?
IT wants everyone’s internet speed test screenshot. Yours is 3 Mbps — fifty times slower than anyone else’s. Questions will follow.
You built a home “call booth” from a fridge box. Quiet inside, but hot and cramped.
This morning is the sports match you’ve waited a year for. It clashes with the monthly department call. The others are fans too.
Once a month HR sends a random employee a lunchtime pizza. Today the courier rings — you didn’t order. You’ve won.
You’re recording a tutorial for colleagues. Halfway through, the cat loudly drinks from your mug. The audio is crystal clear.
Natasha asks on the call: “Why are you always looking sideways?” You’re looking at your second monitor — at your chat with her.
You ordered a desk lamp; a garden gnome arrived. The courier insists it’s your order. The gnome is smiling.
left: Keep the gnome on your desk

text: A colleague on a call asks to borrow money “till payday” and sends bank details right away. You barely know each other.
At the end of an online interview the candidate asks: “Can I see your office?” There isn’t one. Behind you: the kitchen, stove and a sock-laden airer.
Your laptop sits low, so colleagues see only your chin and the ceiling. The manager jokes he can see “a new chandelier.”
The company livestreams its anniversary. You’re asked to give a toast “on behalf of remote staff.” There are a hundred of you.
A photo shoot for an ad is happening at the coworking space. The photographer asks you to “work naturally” while smiling into the camera.
A colleague on the other side of the world sets a task “due end of day.” His end of day is your 4 am.
A colleague went on holiday with an auto-reply: “For everything, contact [your name].” Nobody warned you. Your inbox is flooded.
Fifteen people in the project chat, two talking, the rest reacting 👍. You can’t tell if they understand anything.
For the fifth time this evening you open the fridge “for a little break.” Nothing has changed in there. Nor in you.
Your partner suggests no laptop this weekend. You agree. On Saturday morning you catch yourself with it on your lap.
Raya admits on a call she hasn’t gone further than the corner shop in a month. Neither have you. She suggests a walk together.
Colleagues invite you to an online game. The manager’s playing too. You accidentally knock him out in round one.
Your neighbour asks if you need anything from the shop, “since you’re always working.” It feels awkward, but you are out of bread.
You decided to “just check email” in bed. Two hours later you’re still there, report finished and next week planned.
A courier delivers at 11 pm and wakes everyone. It’s the laptop stand you ordered at 3 am a week ago.
In the evening company podcast they talk about you: “The person who always replies first.” You’re not sure it’s a compliment.
HR sent candles “for cosy evenings after work.” The box says “Scent: Fresh Office.” It smells of paper and coffee.
Your sister asks to stay for a week: “You’re home anyway, it’ll be fun.” It’s your project deadline week.
right: Ask her to come next week

text: An 11 pm call with a team on the other side of the world. You’re in pyjamas and cameras are on. They’re in business attire — it’s their morning.
An evening notification: “Your manager rated your week 4 out of 5.” No comment. It’s a new system.
A friend from another city video-calls to chat. Five minutes in, you catch yourself wanting to ask him for “an agenda.”
right: Admit work’s stuck in your head

text: The team lead sends a survey: “What gets in the way of remote work?” “Your morning calls” isn’t an option, but there’s an “Other” box.
One wireless earbud has vanished. Call in half an hour. The cat looks suspiciously pleased, sitting by the sofa.
At 7 a colleague four hours ahead rings: “Oh, did I wake you? Thought it was midday for you.” He needs the shared drive password.
The company sent an ergonomic chair to assemble. The manual has 64 steps and no words, just pictures.
The new system asks for an app code every 15 minutes. Your phone is charging in another room.
A client writes: “As agreed on yesterday’s call…” You recall no such call. It isn’t in your calendar either.
Leadership declares a “no-meeting week.” By Monday morning you’re in three “optional discussion sessions.”
Your region doesn’t change clocks; your team’s does. As of today all your meetings have shifted an hour.
Petya sends you a detailed weekend report with photos. Forty-six of them. Plus: “Chat over coffee?”
The electricians warn of a 15-minute power cut at 10. That’s the climax of your presentation. Laptop charged, router not.
You’ve been asked to cover the support chat from 7 because a colleague is ill. You sleepily greet a client with “Good night.”
left: Laugh about it with the client

text: You bought a 4K webcam. Colleagues say they can see their own reflections in your glasses — and the screen with their messages.
You registered for an online learning conference. It starts at 6 am your time. No recordings.
During a call with your manager, a robocall offers a “free water filter check.” It plays through the speakers.
Mitya wants a camera-free Friday. The manager objects: “We need to see faces.” The team waits for your view.
You type in the client chat: “Honestly, he’s such a bore.” It was meant for a colleague, about a different client. The client is silent.
You decide on a 15-minute pause. The moment you stand, a video call: “Just a tiny question.” You sit back down.
At a time-management session the trainer says: “Turn off all notifications.” A minute later twenty pop up on her screen.
A courier asks you to accept a parcel for a neighbour who’s out. It’s a huge box and something inside beeps every five minutes.
A remote team lead role opens up. Your lead hints you should apply — “though it means more calls.”
There’s a teammate nobody has ever seen or heard: he only replies in chat. The manager asks you to “check he’s OK.”
A data sheet came with dates in US format. You swapped month and day in the board report. It’s already sent.
A colleague proposes daily video lunches. Today he eats while describing his renovation in exhaustive detail.
Builders outside your window wave at you at your laptop. One gives a thumbs-up whenever you say something inspiring on a call.
A colleague shares his screen; his wallpaper is a photo of your manager captioned “Onward to the goal!” The manager sees it too.
You bought an exercise bike and put it by the desk. This evening you notice laundry drying on it. The bike doesn’t mind.
The team holds an online board-game night. You’re paired with the manager, who is fiercely competitive.
Your teenage son offers to set up a “proper streamer camera and lighting” — price: a week without a gaming ban.
Your family video-calls every Sunday. Today you open on autopilot: “Let’s keep it short, I’ve got another at six.”
The quarterly report is done. You hit send at 6:59 pm. At 7:00 the manager’s auto-reply: “On leave until Monday.”
The cat fell asleep on your lap at 6 pm. Standing up means waking him. Work remains, and the laptop is a metre away.
A friend takes you to the gym. You realise the last time you saw this many people was on an all-hands call, in little boxes.
The team ships an update at 11 pm when traffic is low. You’re asked to “just be reachable.” Reachable means awake.
You completed an online course: “How to Say No.” The very next evening the manager asks you to take on another task.
A photographer neighbour offers to shoot a “professional avatar” for you. You’ve had a cat avatar for three years.
In the evening you write tomorrow’s to-do list. It’s longer than today’s, though you worked all day.
Your child graduates from nursery online. The ceremony is at 6 pm — the same time as a call the CEO booked.
At 9 the bot asks: “What are you working on today?” You type “myself.” It logs that as a task due Friday.
A coworking regular greets everyone loudly by name each morning. For three days he’s called you “our accountant,” though you’re a designer.
Out of habit you packed lunch in a box, like for the office. It’s in the fridge a metre from your desk. It feels weird.
Every morning Lyuba books 15 minutes of “team coffee.” Today only you came. She’s thrilled and tells you all about her cat.
The manager calls at 8:15 and, without hello, says: “You up to speed?” You’ve seen nothing. You just got up.
Window cleaners arrive at 9 and stand right behind your glass with rags and buckets. You’re on a call with a new partner; the camera faces the window.
left: Turn the camera to the wall

text: Forty unread chats this morning. One is a surprise party for your birthday, organised by colleagues. The surprise is blown.
You aimed to get to the coworking space by 8 for a window seat. At 7:55 there’s a queue of six laptop warriors.
Vova posts 15 cat GIFs in the team chat. A minute later the manager writes: “Let’s agree not to spam.” Vova DMs: “Back me up?”
On the call you see the manager talking, but there’s no audio. You rejoin. Still nothing. Everyone else nods. Apparently it’s just you.
You’re so used to coffee on calls you’re up to six cups a day. This morning your hand reaches for a seventh.
Your child has a morning show at school and parents are invited. It clashes with a client call you’ve already moved twice.
A neighbour posts in the building chat: “Drilling 9 to noon, sorry remote folks.” You appreciate the warning, but your project review is at 10.
A colleague on a call is in a café, and through the window behind him you can see your own building. Turns out he lives opposite.
A client suggests lunch at a restaurant near you. You agree, but forget how in-person meetings work: you keep reaching for a mute button.
The company is refreshing its website and wants a professional photo by 3 pm. You only have a holiday shot in a panama hat and one with the cat.
A client leaves public feedback on the company site: “Great specialist, though always eating on calls.” Everyone can see it.
You’re in 74 work chats. Missing something important is a matter of time. The manager complains you don’t reply.
You and a colleague are editing the same deck. He deletes slides; you restore them. He deletes again. Neither of you writes a word.
A corporate online quiz asks: “What’s the manager’s cat called?” You know — the cat attends every call.
Your desk lamp flickers like a strobe during your presentation. Colleagues type: “Is this a disco?” The manager: “Do something.”
An unexpected one-hour gap appears in your calendar — the first this week. That minute a colleague writes: “Yay, you’re free? Can you help?”
Grandma video-calls in work hours to show you her tomatoes. She doesn’t know you’re with a client. Second attempt.
The director DMs you one word: “Pop in.” Pop in where? There’s no office. A call, presumably. But which?
Sasha keeps posting “anyone around?” It always means “help with a broken file.” Today it’s you replying… again.
A neighbour invites you to a beginners’ dance class: “You sit all day.” You haven’t danced since graduation, and tomorrow is another day of calls.
The company runs an online party for staff children. Your kid insists you sit beside him the whole hour. Your report is half done.
You decided your phone goes on Do Not Disturb after 7 pm. By 7:05 you’ve checked it three times.
On an evening walk you see dozens of windows with people glowing blue at laptops. You’re a bit glad you’re not one of them right now.
In the evening Nailya writes: “Mind if I use your idea in my presentation tomorrow? I’ll credit you!” It’s a good idea.
You order a second monitor in the evening. A minute later, from your partner: “Did you just order another screen?” You share an account.
Your partner’s away, so you eat in front of the laptop. Twenty minutes later you’re answering emails and the food’s cold.
The team ordered pizza for a Friday evening video hangout. Yours arrives last, as everyone finishes and logs off.
You must write a review of a colleague by 8 pm. You’ve only chatted. All you know is he uses a lot of 🔥.
You dream you walk into the office and everyone has their cameras off — paper bags on their heads. You wake at 3 am.
left: Share the dream with the team

text: You’re on holiday, and colleagues added you to a new chat: “Urgent before Monday.” It already has 80 messages.
You bought a lamp that switches to warm light in the evening “so your brain knows work’s over.” Your brain didn’t get the memo and wants email.
You’re working from a village. At 6 the neighbour’s cow wakes you, at 7 the rooster, at 8 a tractor. At 9 stand-up, where everyone moans about sleep.
HR sends a daily “motivational quote.” Today: “Work isn’t a place, it’s a state of mind.” Your state of mind is going back to bed.
The nursery has shut for a week. Your child is overjoyed; you have five calls today. Grandma lives in another city.
right: Work with the kid beside you

text: You accidentally set your messenger status to “On holiday 🏖.” All morning nobody writes, and it’s blissful. At 11 the manager asks why you didn’t mention your leave.
This morning your voice assistant heard “cancel all meetings today” and did it. You said “cancel the alarm.”
The guard from the closed office calls: “Your plant’s still here, want it?” Your ficus — you’d completely forgotten it.
right: Ask him to give it away

text: Your laptop charger starts sparking this morning. A new one arrives tomorrow. You’re at 70% with a day of calls.
The call app auto-transcribed stand-up. Your yawn came out as “AAAAWW, well well” and went to all attendees.
right: Ask for it to be deleted

text: A client writes at 7:30: “Small change?” The change: redo everything. Delivery is today at noon.
Lilya asks in the team chat: “Does anyone know how to unsubscribe from all company mailings?” The manager reacts 🤨.
Karina joins stand-up holding her baby, who starts crying. She DMs you: “Please run it for me.” You’ve prepared nothing.
You record a screencast for a client and accidentally include 10 minutes of you staring at the screen, sighing. It’s already sent.
right: Hope he doesn’t watch it all

text: You’re invited to a client’s office. Security wants ID; all you have is your cat avatar in the work messenger.
right: Run the meeting by video from reception

text: Two departments argue in the shared chat about who blew the deadline. Both tag you: “Confirm it was them!” You know it was everyone.
Colleagues made a sticker pack from your call screenshots. The favourite shows you yawning. It’s used on all the manager’s messages.
The company now delivers lunches to remote staff. Yours arrived at 4 pm — cold, with a note: “Enjoy your lunch!”
For the annual report HR is making a collage of call screenshots. In every frame with you, you’re either blinking or chewing.
Your child doodles in your work notebook during a call. The back has your report notes. Now it also has a rocket.
The postman brings a registered letter during a call. You mime “one minute”; he mimes “three, max.”
Edik is on a call from his car again. Parking, pulling out, honking. Today he’s also refuelling. Agenda: the annual budget.
Behind the wall, your partner loudly calls his boss “our general” on his call. Your manager, on yours, laughs and asks who that is.
right: Ask your partner to pipe down

text: The company asks how many hours a day you spend on calls. You count honestly: 6.5 — more than you slept last night.
An older colleague asks how to react to messages. He carefully writes in a notebook: “Heart — for approval.”
Your new work desk won’t fit through the room door. The courier’s gone. You and the desk are in the hall at 8 pm.
At 8 pm Gena posts his new triple-monitor home office: “Finally I can work at full power!” You share a project tomorrow.
right: Ask him not to work nights

text: An online coach sends an evening exercise: “Close your eyes for 5 minutes.” You wake up at 11 pm.
A colleague retires after 30 years with an online send-off. You’re asked to arrange a gift that can be posted within two days.
The neighbour’s cat came over the balcony again and claimed your chair. You realise he spends more time with you than you do with people.
Exhausted, you curl up on the sofa under a blanket with the laptop. A minute later a client video-calls.
The manager launches an evening stream: “I answer your questions.” The only person asking is his mum.
The team meets in person at a café for the first time. Everyone sits on their phones, messaging each other in the work chat.
Your favourite colleague is leaving. On the farewell call he says he’ll miss your chat jokes. You didn’t know he read them.
Your partner proposes swapping work rooms monthly “to be fair.” His faces north and is cold; yours gets the sun.
The upstairs neighbours bought a smart speaker and do workouts to loud music every morning at 8:30. The floor shakes; your mic hears it all.
A new colleague DMs everyone: “Hi! Tell me about yourself in three sentences.” You can’t describe yourself before coffee.
The manager is 15 minutes late to his own call. Everyone sits silent; nobody dares leave. You host the next call in 15 minutes.
You’re on the bus to the coworking space, joining stand-up from your phone. The driver announces stops louder than you can talk.
Your partner baked a pie this morning “for your colleagues.” They’re in five cities. He can’t fathom not treating the team.
Your laptop camera died. On calls you’re now the passport photo the system auto-loaded. It’s ten years old.
The bulb in your workroom has blown. No spare. On calls you’re lit only by your screen and look blue.
You’ve decided to start days phone-free: 30 minutes of breakfast and the window. At 8:05 the manager rings your landline.
You join a meeting; only one other person is there — a colleague you don’t know, also waiting. You both stay silent. Five minutes pass.
A courier brings company gifts “for a year of remote work”: logo socks and a voucher for an hour in a massage chair you don’t own.
You take handwritten notes on a call but can’t read them after. “Buy… cat?… report…” The manager asks for the summary.
The neighbour starts vacuuming at 7 am. You’ve endured it, but today you have a call with another time zone at exactly 7.
A candidate joins the interview from a gym treadmill. He says he “values time.” He’s out of breath by question two.
The team’s shared tracking spreadsheet was deleted overnight. By whom — unknown. The bin is empty.
right: Wait for IT to restore it

text: The team lead wants everyone to post a weather emoji each morning “to feel connected.” It’s foggy outside. There’s no fog emoji.
You set your alarm to 8:45, since there’s no commute. Today you were on a call by 8:46 — a new record.
Nika writes: “Thanks for yesterday! Sent you a pizza.” It arrives at 8 am while you’re asleep. The courier keeps ringing.
right: Ask him to leave it outside

text: A new pilot: everyone hosts a weekly video “open-door hour.” Nobody came to yours. The hour has passed.
A courier brings someone else’s lunch: sushi for “Sales team, 12 people.” Your address must still be in the system as the old office.
You spent two hours on an important email. It didn’t send: “No internet connection.” The draft didn’t save.
In a meeting everyone says “let’s pause and reflect.” That means another call tomorrow. And the day after.
Your email AI suggests a reply: “Thanks! With love, your colleague.” You nearly hit send to your manager.
A neighbour knocks: his laptop died and he wants to work at yours “for a couple of hours.” Your calls start at 2.
Timur shares his screen and you spot a video tab: “How to look busy while remote.” He’s presenting his plans.
Your partner gets home early: “Done for the day?” You’re still on a call and wave; he waves back — in frame.
Colleagues propose video email signatures: “Hi, it’s me, have a great day!” The manager loves it.
An unknown number: “Hello! You’re in the running for ‘Remote Worker of the Month,’ we need your video.” Sounds fishy.
You submit a report. The manager replies: “Good. But let’s discuss on a call.” The call lasts an hour. Decision: “Leave it as is.”
A colleague wants a photo of your cat for a team slide, “Our Helpers.” The cat refuses to pose and turns away.
left: Chase the shot for half an hour
right: Send a photo of his back

text: The coworking space offers you a “promotion”: a window seat, for a fee. You’ve been coming a year and feel you’ve earned it free.
You’re back from a week working at the dacha. Tonight the neighbour texts: “You left your laptop here!” You thought it was in your bag.
You invented an end-of-day ritual: say “see you tomorrow” to the laptop and close the lid. Your partner filmed it and wants to show friends.
The manager wants tomorrow’s task list every evening. Tonight’s list is longer than the energy you had today.
A friend takes you to the theatre. In the interval you reply to your manager and miss the bell for act two.
At bedtime your child asks why you say “see you tomorrow” on calls to people you’ve never actually seen.
At 9:30 pm Zakhar writes: “Mind if I book a call Saturday? Just half an hour.” Saturday is your mum’s birthday.
A colleague suggests nightly online chess “to unwind.” You lose your third game in a row; your brain is not unwound.
In the evening someone asks who can help with an urgent task. Silence. It’s squarely your area of expertise.
The company sent everyone sweets on Friday evening for finishing the project. You got two boxes — yours and a colleague’s with a similar surname.
You’re a guest on an evening podcast about remote work. The host asks: “What’s hardest?” You answer honestly: “Closing the laptop.”
You decide to change your desktop wallpaper. An hour later you’re still choosing between mountains, sea and the cat.
Your schoolboy son asks why you say “Team, let’s sync up” on calls. He wants to say it to his friends.
You charge your phone in the kitchen at night to avoid chats. At 2 am you get up “for water” and read chats.
A barista neighbour invites you to work at his café in the quiet evenings: “You’re remote, right?” You wanted to rest.
Unable to sleep, you decide to “do a little work.” By 2 am you’ve finished tomorrow’s tasks. Your call is at 8.
It snowed overnight and for the first time in a month you want to go out in the morning. Stand-up is in 40 minutes. The snow is gorgeous.
The company booked an online ergonomist to check your workspace. At 8:30 he asks you, on video, to tape-measure your desk, chair and elbows.
You must drop the car at the garage this morning, and there’s a 9 am call. The waiting room has a blaring TV.
right: Call from the car on the lift

text: The new onboarding bot sends you — five years at the company — a welcome: “Welcome aboard! Here’s where the kitchen is.”
You post a Monday meme in the team chat. The manager replies: “It’s Tuesday.” It’s still funny.
You realise you’ve forgotten what your neighbourhood looks like in daylight: dark mornings, dark evenings, calls in between. Today lunch could be outdoors.
Morning notice: salaries are delayed three days “due to the new remote payroll system.” Rent is due today.
Alisa, one zone ahead, posts “Good morning!” an hour before you start, and all day you feel behind.
They’re laying asphalt under your window. Roller rumbling, workers shouting, smell everywhere. It’s a day of calls.
The manager asks each person for one word on their mood. Everyone says “great.” Your turn.
You find yesterday’s email still sitting in drafts. The recipient asks this morning where it is.
An online class reunion at 8 am your time — it suits classmates scattered across the world. You haven’t seen them in ages.
The department head wants to “be closer to people” and now phones everyone personally for 5 minutes each morning. Your slot is 8:40.
You paid for morning online fitness. The trainer says: “Cameras on, I can see you!” Behind you hangs the suit for tomorrow’s meeting.
A courier rings at 7:30: “I have your order but my van broke down. Can you collect it one street over?” It’s your new keyboard.
The team lead asks: keep daily stand-up or switch to twice a week? Open vote. The team lead adores stand-ups.
The dog has learned to open your study door. At 9:05 each morning he wanders into frame looking like “was I invited?”
You learn this morning the project deadline moved a week earlier. It was announced in one of 12 chats — the one you’re not in.
In a teamwork session you’re paired for a “trust exercise”: give your partner control of your screen for 10 minutes.
Three hours of back-to-back calls in, you realise you can’t remember what the first was about. You chaired it.
right: Claim it’s all in your head

text: Someone at the coworking space left their stuff on your favourite desk and vanished two hours ago. You’re perched on the windowsill.
A colleague leaves 40 public comments on your doc. Each one starts with “Don’t take this the wrong way, but…”
A notice from the post office: a parcel held at customs. You must go in work hours. The queue is two hours long.
You’re offered a project with a team abroad. You’d work their hours, but it’s interesting and comes with a bonus.
While you demo, the client’s child in a superhero costume leaps off the sofa behind him. He acts like nothing’s happening.
At a café the waiter asks about dessert. You reply on autopilot: “Let’s circle back to that next week.”
Vanya sends a voice note: “So, it’s a long story…” Duration: 14 minutes.
right: Ask for three lines in text

text: The manager says: “If you disagree, stay silent.” Everyone stays silent. You’re not sure you understood the voting rules.
You’re helping your mum set up her new phone. She ends up in your work messenger and posts “Hello?” in your team chat.
You must fill in your timesheet. For “2 pm to 3 pm,” you honestly can’t remember.
A neighbour asks: “You know the internet, right? Why’s mine so slow?” You check his router — it’s connected to your Wi-Fi.
The manager rings: “I need you to give the client presentation for me, in 10 minutes.” You’re in pyjamas and don’t know the topic.
You want quiet tonight, but the upstairs neighbours are watching a film in surround sound. After a day of voices, it’s the last straw.
left: Ask them to turn it down

text: A childhood friend will pass through your city tomorrow afternoon. You’re booked with calls, but it’s been five years.
right: Meet in the evening for an hour

text: Colleagues recorded a congratulations video for your promotion. Everyone sings off-key but sincerely. The manager loudest of all.
You realise you haven’t said a word aloud all day — everything was in chat. Your voice sounds odd.
You’ve decided to move to a smaller town since work is remote. The manager asks if the internet will be stable there.
In an evening painting class the teacher says: “Paint what surrounds you.” You draw a monitor, a mug and headphones.
HR calls in the evening: “You haven’t taken leave in 14 months. Take next week.” Next week is the project launch.
The team cooks the same dish together on video. Yours burned; everyone else’s worked. Plates are being shown.
Friends plan Saturday. You automatically write: “I have a window from 2:00 to 2:30.” They’re baffled.
At an evening conference you ask the speaker a question. He replies: “Great question! By the way, want to work for us?”
Your new slippers arrived with lights and sound. Every step beeps. You’re on an evening call.
Masha writes: “I’m drowning, can I hand you one report?” You’ve already taken two others’ reports this week.
You repaint the wall behind your desk to look nicer on calls. At 11 pm you realise the colour is “toxic lime.”
You shut the laptop at 6 pm and went out. An hour later your partner sends a photo: laptop open, 12 new messages.
A retired neighbour invites you for tea: “I’m home all day too, let’s keep each other company.” He tells great stories.
First evening of leave, you open the work messenger “just to check nothing’s on fire.” It is. And you can see who lit it.
At the company’s online party you’re asked for a funny remote-work story. All your stories involve the cat.
In the evening the manager books a 7:30 am call: “Sorry for the early start, but it matters.” You were about to go to bed.
The school parents’ chat asks for “someone who’s home in the day” to help redecorate the classroom on Wednesday. All eyes on you.
At 11:40 pm you have a brilliant project idea. You want to message your manager, but he gets notifications at night.
Renata proposes a morning “five-minute support circle”: everyone shares what worries them. Three people came, all silent.
You must send the manager a sales summary each morning. Regions report at different times; the last at 10:30.
You covered your laptop camera with a sticker “just in case.” The morning call needs video, and the sticker won’t peel off.
HR runs a “breakfast with leadership.” Submit questions in advance. You send: “When will the internet allowance be paid?”
A client contract must be signed this morning, but the signatory — your manager — has lost his e-signature access. He asks you to “sort it somehow.”
The internet technician arrives at 9 to replace a cable and needs everything off for an hour. You slept well for once and are raring to work.
Your phone fell in the sink this morning. It survived, but the mic crackles. Client call in 20 minutes; the laptop is charging in another room.
At stand-up you describe yesterday’s work and a colleague says: “I did that too.” You both worked on the same thing.
At 8:30 a document arrives with edits from ten people, all contradicting each other. Decision needed by 10.
A newcomer asks in chat if he may work nights because “it’s more productive.” The manager’s still asleep. You’re his mentor.
A courier delivers a parcel meant for a colleague in another city — you’re listed by mistake. Inside: the laptop she needs today.
Leadership asks if you’d like to rent a small three-person office in your city. The other two are colleagues you’ve never met.
You answered a client at 6:30 because you couldn’t sleep. Now he writes at 6:30 every day expecting an instant reply.
The team suggests a weekly trip to a countryside coworking space. Departure at 7 am. Fun, but early.

At 9 the client sends a blurry photo of his whiteboard plan, all jumbled. He asks you to “build it like the board.”
The morning after a night release, the team meets for a retrospective. Everyone’s exhausted; nobody wants to start.
You’re cat-sitting for a colleague on holiday. The cat sits in front of the camera every call. Everyone assumes it’s yours.
You’re negotiating with a supplier on video. Behind him someone asks loudly: “Well, have you squeezed them yet?” He turns red.
The manager introduces a tracker where everyone logs mood as a colour. The whole team has been “green” for three days. You’re “yellow.”
Yaroslav asks you to check his presentation for leadership. Sixty slides, talk in an hour. He’s nervous.
On a lunchtime walk you run into a colleague from another department. You recognise each other by voice. He suggests coffee.
You’re presenting. The key-figures slide won’t open: “File corrupted.” Everyone waits; the manager raises an eyebrow.

text: Friends invite you on a weekend hike with no signal. The manager asks if you’ll be reachable “at least by text.”
